items.title: “This accident took away my freedom”; Vehicle recovery company fined after worker crushed under truck left unable to walk unaided
items.summary: Simon Pedder was crushed under a reversing recovery truck and now needs crutches, a frame and a wheelchair. More than 10 months on, he has been unable to return to work and says, “life will never be the same”. HSE found the company had no suitable traffic management system and no adequate precautions for reversing […]
items.body:
- Simon Pedder was crushed under a reversing recovery truck and now needs crutches, a frame and a wheelchair.
- More than 10 months on, he has been unable to return to work and says, “life will never be the same”.
- HSE found the company had no suitable traffic management system and no adequate precautions for reversing vehicles – which remain a leading cause of workplace injury.
A Swindon-based vehicle recovery business has been fined after a worker was struck by a reversing vehicle and suffered life-changing injuries.
On 13 June 2025, Simon Pedder was undertaking yard duties at Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited in Highworth when he was suddenly hit and crushed under a company-owned recovery truck.
Mr Pedder suffered fractures to both legs and an arm, a punctured lung and a fractured rib. He was airlifted to the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, where he spent five weeks and underwent several operations to rebuild his legs, including skin grafts.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited had failed to implement a suitable traffic management system to make sure vehicles and pedestrians could circulate safely and had not implemented proper precautions to assist reversing drivers.
(Photographs showing before and after HSE intervention)
More than 10 months later, Mr Pedder’s recovery has not progressed as he had hoped. The extent of his injuries means that in addition to using crutches, a Zimmer frame and wheelchair, Simon now needs regular care visits and cannot carry out basic tasks like getting into the shower without help. He has been told he will most likely need walking aids for the rest of his life.
Describing the impact of the incident on his life, Mr Pedder said:
“I used to be a very sociable person, the life of the party, both in work and with friends; this has been taken away from me as now I spend my days sitting at home by myself. My mood is very low, and this is affecting not only myself but also my family, who say my personality appears to have changed completely.”
He added, “there are many basic things I can’t do, for example, I can’t cut the grass, I can’t fold the washing, I can’t go for a walk, and I am not allowed to drive. This accident took away my freedom.”
He also described the impact on his family, with his wife cutting short her working hours to support his care, and the family rearranging the living room to accommodate a hospital bed. Mr Pedder said: “I feel so bad because I am affecting those who are close to me. My life will never be the same and I feel like this accident should never have happened as I was only doing my job.”
Failure to manage reversing vehicle risks
HSE inspectors found failures by Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited to properly control the risk of reversing vehicles – despite this being one of the leading causes of workplace fatal injury. To manage workplace transport effectively, employers should consider the risks associated with their site and vehicles. Where workers are required to operate on foot in areas where there are moving vehicles, employers must ensure traffic routes are organised in a way that prevents collisions between pedestrians and vehicles.
HSE guidance advises implementing a one-way system for vehicle circulation to eliminate the need for reversing. Where this isn’t possible, the site should be organised to include safety measures such as protective barriers, clear markings and pedestrian crossing points. To aid a driver’s field of vision and alert pedestrians to reversing vehicles, precautionary measures such as rear-view cameras and warning alarms should also be fitted to vehicles.
Guidance on workplace transport safety is freely available on the HSE website: Workplace transport – HSE.
Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited, based at Blackworth Industrial Estate, Highworth, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £28,000 and ordered to pay £2,000 in costs at Bristol Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Laura Artosi said:
“Almost 25 per cent of fatal workplace transport accidents in Great Britain occur while a vehicle is reversing – a stark reminder to employers to properly assess and manage this fundamental risk.
“Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited lacked a suitable traffic management system, including adequate arrangements to ensure vehicles could reverse without risks to those on foot. These failings led to an incident that has robbed Simon Pedder of much of his freedom and will likely have a lasting impact on his life.
“Had Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited implemented robust measures to allow pedestrians and vehicles to move safely across its site, this incident would not have occurred.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Karen Park and paralegal officer Michael Millman.

items.title: Fish processing firm fined almost a quarter of a million pounds after worker’s arm pulled into machine after safety guard left off
items.summary: Worker suffered fractured jaw and chest and arm trauma when he was pulled into a conveyor mechanism A section of fixed guarding had been removed two weeks earlier and not replaced Company’s guarding checks did not include non-electrical fixed guards A Peterhead fish processing company has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into […]
items.body:
- Worker suffered fractured jaw and chest and arm trauma when he was pulled into a conveyor mechanism
- A section of fixed guarding had been removed two weeks earlier and not replaced
- Company’s guarding checks did not include non-electrical fixed guards
A Peterhead fish processing company has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into a machine through a gap where a safety guard should have been.
The man, then aged 30, was working as a chargehand on a production line at Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Limited’s premises in Peterhead on 19 August 2025 when the incident happened.
What happened
The worker had stopped to deal with a box that had jammed too high in a rack loader cage to be reached from the ground. He entered the production line through a gap in the guarding without isolating the power, then climbed onto the conveyor and pressed down on the lid to release the jam. The machine restarted, and his right arm was pulled into the pusher section of the rack loader. Unable to free himself, he was drawn further into the mechanism until his head made contact with moving parts.
A colleague who heard the worker’s shouts for help isolated the power and stopped the machine. The man was taken to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, where he was found to have a fractured jaw and trauma to his chest and right arm. He needed surgery to insert metal plates in his jaw and spent three days in hospital. He returned to work on 29 September 2025 and has made a full recovery.
HSE investigation
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that a section of fixed guarding next to the production line had been removed during maintenance around two weeks before the incident and had not been put back. Without the guard, the gap gave access to the machine without the power being isolated. The correct route in, through an interlocked gate, would have switched off the machinery as soon as the gate was opened.
HSE found that, while the guard was missing, staff had used the gap to reach the machinery on various occasions when boxes jammed, rather than the interlocked gate. Maintenance staff told HSE they had seen the guard missing and had seen employees using the gap, but it was not reinstated. The weekly inspection checklist used by the in-house maintenance team did not include checking the integrity of non-electrical fixed guarding.
Had the guarding been in place, the only way into the machine would have been through the interlocked gate, and the incident would not have happened.
HSE guidance highlights the importance of following safe isolation and lock-off procedures before any maintenance or cleaning work is carried out. Employers must ensure all machinery is properly isolated from power sources, and that systems are regularly monitored and reviewed to prevent inadvertent start-up. Further guidance is available here: The safe isolation of plant and equipment – HSE.
Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Ltd, of East Quay, The Harbour, Peterhead, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) and (2) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 and Section 33(1)(c) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £245,000 and ordered to pay a with a victim surcharge of £18,375, at Peterhead Sheriff Court on 28 October 2026.
HSE inspector Nicky Smith said:
“This was a wholly preventable incident which left a worker seriously injured.
“A missing guard and an unchecked gap left the way open for a worker to be dragged into a machine.
“Guards must be kept in place, and checks must cover every guard, not just the electrical ones.”

items.title: Engineering company fined after worker suffers finger amputation
items.summary: Worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded saw. HSE investigation found the company had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous moving parts. Company fined after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998. An engineering company has been fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation […]
items.body:
- Worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded saw.
- HSE investigation found the company had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous moving parts.
- Company fined after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998.
An engineering company has been fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation after a worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded automatic saw.
Thomas Davies, 21, was working for Dlinexsign Ltd when the incident occurred. Having reached into the machine to retrieve a cut piece of material, his hand came into contact with the moving saw blade, resulting in him losing part of his finger.
The incident occurred at the company’s premises at Buckingham Road Industrial Estate, Brackley. The machine was used to cut lengths of material, and Mr Davies was able to reach into the machine and access the dangerous moving parts while it was operating.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Dlinexsign Ltd had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to the dangerous parts of the machinery.
HSE guidance states that employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. This will normally be achieved using fixed guarding, but where access is required, other protective measures such as interlocked guards may be necessary to ensure dangerous movement has stopped before a person can reach the danger zone.
Further guidance can be found on HSE’s website on the safe use of work equipment: Introduction to machinery safety – HSE.
Dlinexsign Ltd, of Shires Road, Brackley, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation to Mr Davies, and £9,064.34 in prosecution costs at Milton Keynes Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Dulanjala Kandana-Arachchige said:
“This incident demonstrates the serious consequences that can result when access to dangerous parts of machinery is not effectively prevented.
“Employers must ensure that machinery is properly guarded and that effective measures are in place to prevent workers from reaching dangerous moving parts.
“This was a preventable incident. Employers have a responsibility to ensure that work equipment can be used safely and that workers are protected from dangerous machinery.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Tom Ledden-Rocks and paralegal officer Natalie Ellis.

items.body:
Neutral Citation: [2026] UKFTT 01496 (TC)
Taylor House, London
VALUE ADDED TAX – attribution of input tax – whether photography and modelling costs had a direct and immediate link with exempt supplies of credit as well as taxable supplies of goods - apportionment of residual marketing costs between taxable and exempt supplies – whether standard turnover method gave rise to distortions – whether alternative methods guaranteed a more precise apportionment –Article 1, Article 168, Article 173 and Article 174 of the Principal VAT Directive 2006/112/EC – Ss24-26 Value Added Tax Act 1994 – Regulations 101-102B Value Added Tax Regulations 1995 - powers of the Tribunal in relation to an appeal against HMRC's refusal to accept a proposed partial exemption special method – powers of the Tribunal in relation to an appeal against assessments following the issue by HMRC of a standard method override notice – whether assessments made out of time –– s73(6) Value Added Tax Act 1994
Heard on: 22-25 September 2026
Judgment date: 28 October 2026
Before
TRIBUNAL JUDGE ROBIN VOS
MR MOHAMMED FAROOQ
Between
FRASERS GROUP FINANCIAL SERVICES LIMITED
Appellant
and
THE COMMISSIONERS FOR HIS MAJESTY’S REVENUE AND CUSTOMS
Respondents
Representation:
For the Appellant: VALENTINA SLOANE KC of counsel, instructed by Eversheds Sutherland (International) LLP
For the Respondents: HOWARD WATKINSON of counsel, instructed by the General Counsel and Solicitor to HM Revenue and Customs
DECISION
Introduction
These appeals concern the extent to which, for VAT purposes, marketing costs incurred by the appellant related to taxable supplies made by it rather than supplies which were exempt from VAT. This in turn determines the amount of VAT incurred in relation to those costs which can be claimed as a credit against the VAT charged on the taxable supplies.
The appellant is currently known as Frasers Group Financial Services Limited. However, during the period relevant to these appeals (July 2018 to March 2022), it was known as Studio Retail Limited. The parties therefore refer to the appellant as “Studio” and we will do the same.
During the relevant period, Studio sold a wide range of goods (including for example clothes, gifts, toys and homeware) through catalogues and online. Most customers paid for the goods on credit and the majority of customers incurred interest.
The supplies of the goods themselves are within the scope of VAT whereas the supplies of credit, represented by the interest charged, are exempt from VAT. This is why it is necessary to examine whether certain costs incurred by Studio related both to the taxable supplies of goods and the exempt supplies of credit and, if so, how the costs should be apportioned between those supplies.
Studio has appealed against a number of assessments made by HMRC who have taken the view that the costs should be apportioned by reference to the proportion of the total income of Studio generated by taxable supplies compared to the proportion of that income which relates to exempt supplies (often referred to as the standard turnover method). This results in approximately £2.7m of VAT each year being irrecoverable.
Studio has put forward two main arguments in support of its appeal against the assessments. The first is that, what it refers to as photography and modelling costs (i.e. the cost of producing the photographs of the goods which appear in the catalogues and online) relate only to the supply of goods and not to the supplies of credit so that the VAT incurred in respect of those costs should be recoverable in full. This would result in approximately £60,000 a year of additional input VAT being allowed as a credit.
Studio's second point is that the standard turnover method produces distortions in relation to the apportionment of marketing (but not other) costs between taxable and exempt supplies. It originally put forward five alternative methods of apportioning such costs. However, by the end of the hearing, Studio only pursued two of these alternative methods, one of them subject to modification compared to the proposal put forward prior to the hearing. If either of these proposed alternatives were accepted by the Tribunal, the irrecoverable VAT would be reduced to around £2.3m-£2.5m a year.
There is a further appeal against a decision by HMRC to reject a partial exemption special method (“PESM”) proposed by Studio in 2023 (the “2023 PESM”). This is one of the proposed methods of apportioning the input costs put forward by Studio in its appeal against the various assessments and is the method which Studio seeks to amend.
It does not appear that the appeal against the refusal of the 2023 PESM will have any financial impact separate from the appeals against the assessments themselves although we must of course determine the appeal against the refusal of the 2023 PESM as a separate matter.
In relation to two specific assessments (for the 09/19 and 03/20 VAT periods), Studio argues that the assessments were made outside the statutory time limit and are therefore not valid.
Procedural matters
We should mention that, as well as abandoning its reliance on some of the alternative methods of apportioning costs between taxable and exempt supplies, Studio also indicated prior to the hearing that it would not pursue two other aspects of its appeals.
The first relates to the allocation of costs relating to a call centre in the Philippines between taxable and exempt supplies (appeal number TC/2023/09403). Studio now accepts that these costs should be allocated using the standard turnover method adopted by HMRC when making the assessments.
The second point which Studio no longer pursues is an appeal which had been made against HMRC's refusal of a proposed partial exemption special method put forward in 2022 (appeal number TC/2023/09854).
It follows that these two appeals are dismissed.
In its grounds of appeal, Studio had also argued that in making the assessments HMRC had not applied “best judgment”. Ms Sloane however clarified at the hearing that this is not relied on as a separate ground of appeal but is simply a reflection of Studio’s challenge to HMRC’s refusal to countenance any basis of apportionment between taxable and exempt supplies other than the standard turnover method. We do not therefore deal with this as a separate issue.
At the end of June 2026, HMRC applied for a stay of these appeals pending the final resolution of any appeals relating to the decision of the First-tier Tribunal in Littlewoods Limited v HMRC [2025] UKFTT 01602 (TC). That case dealt with the attribution of photography and modelling costs in similar circumstances to this case.
The stay application was however refused on the basis that these appeals deal not only with the attribution of photography and modelling costs but also the wider apportionment of costs between taxable and exempt supplies. It was in any event noted that questions of attribution are highly fact specific and the outcome of one case will not necessarily determine the outcome of another.
There was some suggestion in the papers provided to the Tribunal that the appeals against some of the assessments might have been made outside the statutory thirty day time limit. To the extent that there are any late appeals, HMRC do not object to them. In any event it seems that the late appeals relate to the appeal against the call centre assessment and the refusal of the 2022 PESM which are not pursued.
If any other appeals are out of time we give permission for the appeals to be notified to the Tribunal outside the statutory time limit as, having considered all the circumstances, it would not in our view be consistent with the overriding objective of dealing with cases fairly and justly to refuse permission some three years after the appeals have been notified to the Tribunal, at the start of the substantive hearing of the appeals and in circumstances where HMRC do not object.
We should record that we raised with Mr Watkinson, appearing for HMRC, the length of his skeleton argument which ran to 88 pages (compared to 42 pages for Ms Sloane, representing Studio), noting the comment of the Tribunal in Hackett v HMRC [2024] UKFTT 00749 (TC) at [19] that there was "nothing skeletal” about a 58 page skeleton argument.
We appreciate that such a document (which, in reality, contains detailed submissions rather than an outline of the points to be made and the authorities relied on) may be helpful to the Tribunal and may reduce the need for lengthy oral submissions. However, we do not think it appropriate for a party to provide the Tribunal with a document which clearly is not a skeleton argument without first explaining to the Tribunal why such a document is felt to be appropriate and seeking permission to do so.
We have been informed that HMRC has made further assessments for the VAT periods 06/22-04/23 and that Studio has notified appeals against these assessments to the Tribunal. Those appeals have however been stayed pending the outcome of these appeals as the issues are materially identical. We do not therefore address those appeals although we appreciate that the outcome of Studio’s appeals against those assessments is likely to be informed by our decision.
THE EVIDENCE
We were provided with a number of bundles of documents and correspondence amounting in total to approximately 5,000 pages as well as various spreadsheets in electronic format. We were also given links to some YouTube videos which gave examples of Studio's television advertising.
The documents included witness statements from three individuals, all of whom gave oral evidence and were cross-examined at the hearing.
We have no doubt that all three witnesses were honest in the evidence they gave and were doing their best to assist the Tribunal. There are however a few points we should mention in relation to their evidence.
Evidence on behalf of HMRC was given by Mr Robin Williamson. This evidence related to the suggestion that some of the assessments had been made out of time which, as we shall see, depends on the opinion of the assessing officer. Although Mr Williamson was an important part of the team dealing with HMRC's inquiries, he was not the assessing officer in relation to any of the assessments in question. We have therefore needed to consider whether we can make inferences based on his evidence and the other evidence before us.
Mr Paul Kendrick (the Managing Director/CEO of Studio at the relevant time) gave evidence on behalf of Studio. There were a number of areas where the evidence given in his witness statement was shown to be incorrect or incomplete. He dealt with two of these points prior to cross-examination. There were however other points which only came to light during cross-examination.
The position in relation to Mr Sam Jones (Director of Finance at Studio during the relevant period), is similar. Some errors in his witness statement were corrected before cross-examination but others were revealed during the course of cross-examination.
These inconsistencies did not in our view affect the credibility of either Mr Kendrick or Mr Jones as witnesses. As we have said, we are entirely satisfied that they were being truthful. Instead, we attribute the inaccuracies in some cases to lapses of memory and in other cases to the fact that Mr Kendrick and, particularly, Mr Jones did not have detailed involvement in some of the marketing activities in question. It does however mean that, where relevant, we have placed more reliance on the documentary evidence.
BACKGROUND FACTS
There is no real dispute between the parties in relation to the underlying facts which are relevant to these appeals. The question is rather how the relevant legal principles relating to the attribution and apportionment of costs for VAT purposes should be applied in the light of those facts.
The factual background is particularly important. As has been noted in many of the cases to which we were referred, small factual differences can lead to different outcomes (see, for example, David Richards LJ in Royal Opera House Covent Garden Foundation v HMRC [2021] EWCA Civ 910 at [3]).
Background to the business
As we have previously explained, Studio's business involved selling a wide range of goods both through catalogues and online. It had no physical shops.
Studio offered its customers a credit account known as Studio Pay and was regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority in respect of this part of its business. Studio Pay operated a little like a credit card in that customers had to make a minimum payment each month (the higher of £10 and 6% of the outstanding balance) and interest was incurred if the full balance was not paid off by a set date. If a customer failed to make the minimum payment, they ceased to receive any marketing materials and would not be permitted to order any further goods.
The rates of interest charged on the credit account were high, although depended on the individual customer. The typical APR was 49.9% (subsequently reduced to 39.9%). The actual APR charged to individual customers varied between 24.9% and 64.9%.
Due to the regulatory environment, Studio had to be careful in marketing Studio Pay. It could not, for example, encourage customers to incur interest or to go into default.
Studio nonetheless encouraged customers to open a credit account. This was not just because a credit account was likely to generate interest income but also because customers with a credit account placed more orders and spent more money whether or not they in fact paid any interest.
The business was significant. It had around two million customers and total revenues which varied between around £390m-£580m during the period in question. Approximately 90% of all purchases were made on credit account. Only about 15% of customers paid off their balances in full each month and so 85% of credit account customers incurred interest. On average, customers with a credit account paid off about 12% of their balance each month.
Both parts of the business were important, with credit interest during the relevant period consistently amounting to approximately 20%-24% of total revenues.
Although Studio has various performance metrics relating to interest income, it is not able to track the precise amount of interest generated by a particular purchase given that the balance of a customer’s credit account fluctuates all the time due to repayments and new orders.
Studio freely acknowledges that its business model was to provide integrated supplies of goods and credit. There was a symbiotic relationship between the two. As Mr Kendrick explained, Studio's ideal customer was one who made regular orders, made use of the credit account and paid interest. The purchase of goods on credit led to predictable and significant interest income whilst customers who had a credit account purchased more goods than other customers. Studio's figures show that credit account customers made three to four purchases a year, that the average order was £75 and that the average annual spend by customers with a credit account was £250.
Studio’s marketing materials
Studio marketed its supplies of goods and of credit in a number of ways. The primary marketing was through the regular catalogues which were sent to existing or prospective customers and through its website.
In addition, Studio also distributed promotional leaflets (which might, for example, be sent to customers with their monthly credit account statement) and emails. Some of these separate marketing materials focused more on the credit side of the business.
Studio also offered promotional deals for Studio Pay, such as an "interest saver" promotion, which allowed a customer a grace period of, say, three months before having to pay any interest. These promotional offers were referenced in all of the types of marketing we have mentioned.
All of these marketing channels used the photographs of the goods to which the photography and modelling costs relate.
As well as these marketing materials, Studio produced television advertisements. Contrary to their witness statements, both Mr Kendrick and Mr Jones confirmed in their oral evidence that the photography and modelling costs used to create photographs of products for the catalogue, leaflets and website were not used in relation to the television advertisements, which were produced entirely separately. We accept this evidence. These advertisements are not therefore relevant when considering whether the photography and modelling costs were used in relation to the supplies of credit.
Studio accepts that all of its marketing materials promote both the supply of goods and the supply of credit and that, with the exception of the photography and modelling costs, all of those costs therefore need to be apportioned between taxable and exempt supplies. We do not therefore need to deal individually with each category of marketing cost other than the photography and modelling costs, which Studio maintains were used only in relation to its supplies of goods and not credit.
In order to determine these appeals, we need to look in a bit more detail at the nature of the various marketing materials. We start with the catalogues which each ran to several hundred pages and were produced three or four times a year.
The majority of the pages of the catalogues contain photographs of the products which are for sale, a description of the product and the price of the product as well as the website address and a telephone number through which orders could be placed. Most of the pages do not refer to purchasing on credit or to Studio Pay.
There are however a limited number of pages where the words “flexible payments” and “Studio Pay” (contained in a box with a consistent design) are superimposed onto the photograph of a particular product. As noted by Mr Watkinson, these messages tend to appear on the photographs of higher value items, although by no means all of the higher value items include such wording.
This is consistent with Studio's strategy, apparent from its board papers, of using credit to encourage customers to purchase higher priced goods which they would not otherwise be able to afford. Mr Kendrick confirmed in his evidence that some guidance was given to those individuals responsible for designing catalogues and web pages as to where to put the messages promoting credit. Mr Jones also acknowledged that references to Studio Pay in the catalogue are deliberately weighted towards higher value products.
In addition to the references to Studio Pay which appear on the photos of some of the products as described above, the catalogue also contains some separate pages describing Studio Pay in more detail or promoting an “interest saver” offer. These pages do not generally contain any photographs but simply explain how the credit account and/or interest saver promotion works.
Mr Kendrick's unchallenged evidence, which (having reviewed the sample catalogues) we accept, was that only approximately 5% of the pages of the paper catalogues contained both photographs of products and references to credit.
Turning to the website, we did not have a live version of the website which was in use at the relevant time, but had screenshots of numerous pages produced from an archive.
What is presumably a landing page when a customer first enters the website allows a customer to click on a particular category of products, such as “Womens”, “Toys” or “Gifts”. This page contains some photos of a product in the particular category but does not mention credit.
However, the landing page for a particular category such as the “Womens” section has a banner with the words “spread the cost” and offering free delivery and a 20% discount for customers who open a credit account as well as containing options to click on photos which lead to various subcategories (such as “Footwear”, or “Top Brands”). If a customer clicks on the banner, more details of the credit account or the promotion are given.
When a customer clicks on a specific product, they are taken to a page which relates only to that product. The page contains photos of the product, a description of the product and the price. It also has a banner at the top making some reference to Studio Pay and/or credit.
A significant number (well over half) of the individual product pages we were supplied with also contained a box directly underneath the price referring to Studio Pay and with an arrow pointing at the price. A typical example reads “Pay no interest for three months on all orders £50 or more. Representative 39.9% APR variable”. This is accompanied by the Studio Pay logo. The customer is able to click on a link to “learn more” which brings up a box giving more details about how Studio Pay and the interest saver option works.
In addition, underneath the link to add the item to the customer's bag there is a further box relating to delivery, Studio's returns policy and the Studio Pay credit account. The wording for Studio Pay reads “Shop now pay later with a Studio Pay credit account”.
As with the catalogues, the website also contained separate pages explaining the Studio Pay credit account in more detail. Most of these pages do not contain photographs. Based on Mr Kendrick's evidence and the photographs themselves, we accept that, where such pages did include photographs, they were stock photographs and are not photographs of specific products offered by Studio.
We had examples of a number of marketing leaflets. These would typically show photographs of a limited number of products with a brief description and the price of the product together with prominent messages about “spreading the cost”, “Studio Pay”, “flexible payments” and/or interest saver options. Mr Kendrick’s evidence (which we accept as it was not challenged) was that, out of a library of several hundred thousand photographs of Studio’s products, no more than a few hundred would have been used for the purposes of such leaflets.
Background to the assessments and decisions being appealed
For many years, Studio had been using a PESM approved by HMRC in 2005 to determine how much of the VAT paid in respect of its costs which were not attributable exclusively to taxable supplies or to exempt supplies should be recoverable.
On 25 June 2018, HMRC issued a partial exemption special method override notice (“SMON”) under regulation 102A Value Added Tax Regulations 1995 (“VATR”). In accordance with s 102B VATR, this required Studio to determine the amount of recoverable input tax in accordance with the use, or intended use, of goods and services in making taxable supplies.
Towards the end of 2019, HMRC started to investigate the way in which Studio had apportioned its costs between taxable and exempt supplies since the SMON had been issued.
During the course of the investigation, it emerged that in apportioning costs, Studio had only taken into account exempt income in the form of credit interest which, based on various assumptions, was calculated as having been received within 12 months of the sale of the goods giving rise to the payments of interest. In addition, photography and modelling costs had been treated as attributable solely to taxable supplies and so had not been apportioned between taxable and exempt supplies.
Ultimately, HMRC did not accept that the method used by Studio resulted in a fair and reasonable apportionment of its costs between taxable and exempt supplies. As a result, HMRC issued a number of VAT assessments under s 73 Value Added Tax Act 1994 (“VATA”).
The calculations used by HMRC for these assessments took the position that the photography and modelling costs were attributable both to the taxable supplies of goods and the exempt supplies of credit and therefore formed part of the residual costs which had to be apportioned between such taxable and exempt supplies. All of the residual costs were then apportioned based on the standard turnover method using the full amount of income actually received by Studio from taxable supplies and exempt supplies.
The assessments were issued at various times between October 2021 and June 2023 and, together, related to all VAT periods from the 09/18 VAT period to the 03/22 VAT period. Some of the assessments were subsequently reduced. In aggregate, the assessments (as reduced) come to a total of a little over £5.6m. These assessments also included some adjustments in relation to the apportionment of the costs of the call centre in the Philippines. As we have mentioned, Studio does not pursue its appeal in respect of the apportionment of these costs.
As part of its discussions with HMRC, Studio put forward an alternative PESM in 2022 which was rejected by HMRC in August 2022. Although Studio has appealed against HMRC's decision to reject the 2022 PESM, as we have already mentioned, it does not now pursue that appeal.
Studio also proposed a further alternative PESM in 2023 which, in apportioning costs, only took account of interest expected (based on various assumptions) to be generated from sales taking place within the relevant period rather than the actual amounts of exempt interest received in that period. This was also rejected by HMRC in July 2023. Studio has appealed against that decision although, as we shall see, it accepts that the proposal contains an error and invites the Tribunal to uphold the 2023 PESM with some variations.
Issues for the Tribunal
There are a number of issues which we must address. The first is whether the photography and modelling costs are attributable solely to the taxable supplies of goods or whether they are also attributable to the exempt supplies of credit.
The second issue relates to the methodology for the apportionment of residual marketing costs (i.e. those costs accepted as being attributable both to taxable and exempt supplies) between the taxable and exempt supplies. Studio must show that the standard turnover method used by HMRC gives rise to distortions and that one of the methods it proposes more accurately reflects the use made of those costs.
During the course of these proceedings, Studio has put forward three alternative methods of apportioning residual costs between taxable and exempt supplies. It is important to note that these three methods have not been formally proposed to HMRC as partial exemption special methods and, although HMRC has rejected them, there is no decision in respect of these alternative methods against which Studio appeals.
Both parties agree however that these alternative methods are relevant in determining the appeals against the assessments. As we shall see, Studio in fact does not rely in full on any of these three alternative methods but relies on one element which is common to two of the alternatives. This excludes interest paid by customers who are in default as a result of having failed to make the minimum monthly payment in respect of their credit account (referred to by the parties as being in a “non-trading position” as such customers are not permitted to place further orders).
Closely linked to the second issue is the appeal against the 2023 PESM. Studio will need to show that the 2023 PESM guarantees a more precise apportionment of costs between taxable and exempt supplies than the standard turnover method used by HMRC. However, they face an additional hurdle which is whether the Tribunal in any event is able to allow Studio's appeal against HMRC's refusal to accept the 2023 PESM given that Studio seeks to uphold it subject to certain amendments.
The final issue is whether the VAT assessments relating to the 09/19 and 03/20 VAT periods were made within the statutory time limit in section 73 VATA.
Studio bears the burden of proof in respect of all of these issues.
Attribution and Apportionment - Legal Principles
As with the basic facts, the parties are largely agreed as to the legal principles which should be applied by the Tribunal. We shall therefore try to set them out relatively succinctly.
We agree with the parties that EU law remains relevant to the interpretation of VAT legislation despite Brexit (ss 2 and 6 European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 - note that the EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 was not in force at the time relevant to these appeals).
EU legislation
Article 1 of the Principal VAT Directive 2006/112/EC (“PVD”) gives businesses the right to deduct “VAT borne directly by the various cost components” of taxable supplies. This is supplemented by Article 168 PVD which only permits a deduction for VAT paid by a business if the goods or services to which the input VAT relates are “used for the purposes” of taxable output transactions.
Where costs relate both to taxable supplies and exempt supplies, Article 173(1) PVD confirms that it is only the proportion which is attributable to taxable supplies which can be deducted.
The apportionment of costs using the standard turnover method is provided for in Article 174(1) PVD. Article 175 PVD permits the standard turnover method to be applied based on the previous year's transactions but subject to adjustment once the current year transactions are known.
There is however provision for apportionment of costs between taxable supplies and exempt supplies to be based on the use made of the goods and services to which the costs relate (Article 173(2)(c) PVD).
Domestic legislation
The provisions of the PVD are reflected in domestic legislation. Sections 24-26 VATA give an entitlement to credit for input tax used in a person's business to the extent that it is attributable to taxable supplies.
Regulation 101 VATR contains a two stage process for determining whether input tax relates to taxable supplies. The first step is to identify input tax on goods or services which are used exclusively in making either taxable supplies or exempt supplies. Where the goods or services to which the input tax relates are not used exclusively in making either taxable supplies or exempt supplies (including, for example, where the goods or services are used to make both taxable and exempt supplies), the amount of input tax attributable to taxable supplies is to be calculated using the standard turnover method.
HMRC may however approve or direct the use of some other method of apportionment between taxable supplies and exempt supplies (i.e. a PESM - Regulation 102(1) VATR). The taxable person must confirm that the PESM “fairly and reasonably represents the extent to which goods or services are used by or are to be used by him in making taxable supplies” (Regulation 102(9) VATR).
As we have seen, Regulation 102A VATR permits HMRC to serve a notice on a taxpayer if they believe that a PESM does not “fairly and reasonably represent the extent to which goods or services are used by him or are to be used by him in making taxable supplies”. If so, the taxpayer must attribute input VAT to taxable and exempt supplies in a way which reflects such use.
In applying these legislative provisions to the present appeals, the first step is therefore to determine whether the photography and modelling costs are used exclusively in making the taxable supplies of goods or whether they are also used for making exempt supplies of credit (in which case they would form part of the residual costs).
Once it is determined whether or not the photography and modelling costs form part of the residual costs, a determination must be made as to the extent to which those residual costs are used in making taxable supplies.
As can be seen, the focus is very much on identifying how the goods or services to which the input tax relates are used. Guidance on how this should be determined is provided in both EU and domestic case law.
Case law - attribution
In BLP Group PLC v Customs and Excise Commissioners (Case C-4/94) [1995] STC 424, the CJEU explained at [19] that, in order for there to be a right to deduct input VAT “the goods or services in question must have a direct and immediate link with the taxable transactions, and that the ultimate aim pursued by the taxable person is irrelevant in this respect”.
In determining whether there is a direct and immediate link between the input transaction and an output transaction, it is necessary for the Court or Tribunal to consider “the facts of each case before them and to take account of all the circumstances surrounding the transactions at issue” - Midland Bank PLC v Customs and Excise Commissioners (Case C-98/98) [2000] STC 501 at [25].
The goods or services to which input VAT relates may have a direct and immediate link with more than one supply. In Dial-a-Phone Limited v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [2004] EWCA Civ 603, Dial-a-Phone made taxable supplies relating to airtime contracts for mobile phones but also made exempt supplies connected to insurance for mobile phones. Parker LJ noted at [30] that:
“…the fact (if it be the fact) that in the instant case the link between the marketing and advertising costs and DaP’s taxable supplies may be more direct and immediate than the link between those costs and DaP’s exempt supplies does not serve to exclude the possibility that there may nevertheless be a sufficiently direct and immediate link between those costs and the exempt supplies.”
As Articles 168 and 173 PVD make clear, the concept of use is important. However, the authorities also refer to a direct and immediate link between input costs and output transactions (BLP) as well as whether the input costs form a “cost component” of the output transactions (reflecting the words of Article 1 PVD).
In principle, the question as to whether goods or services are used for the purposes of a taxable supply, whether there is a direct and immediate link between the goods or services and the taxable supply or whether the goods or services form a cost component of the taxable supply are all different ways of asking the same question (see the explanation of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House at [17] and [18] and Dial-A-Phone at [28]).
In particular, in looking at whether an input transaction is a cost component of an output transaction, it is not necessary “to identify the cost of the input in the calculation of the price for the output” (HMRC v Hotel La Tour Limited [2025] UKSC 46 at [14]).
As noted by the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House at [17], when determining whether goods or services are used for the purposes of taxable supplies “the taxable person’s purpose is to be objectively ascertained from the facts and circumstances of the transactions, not by investigating the subjective intentions of the taxable person”.
There was some suggestion from Mr Watkinson that a broader approach is now required in considering the purposes for which goods and services are used. In support of this, he refers to the observation of the Supreme Court in Hotel La Tour at [15] that:
“…the CJEU has more recently developed the case law to look more broadly at the use made of a particular input and to link it with the taxable overall business of the trader even though the input seems to be consumed by a specific non-taxable transaction”.
However, that is not the situation here. The question is not whether the photography and modelling costs had a link with Studio’s overall business. The question is whether those costs have a sufficiently direct and immediate link with the supplies of credit as well as the supplies of goods (a distinction drawn by the Supreme Court in Hotel La Tour at [15]).
We note that one of the two cases mentioned in Hotel La Tour in support of the proposition (‘Sveda’ UAB v Valstybinė mokesčių inspekcija prie Lietuvos Respublikos finansų ministerijos (Case C-126/14) [2016] STC 447) was also considered by the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House. The Court of Appeal agreed at [83], that Sveda was dealing with a different issue and did “not herald a new and broader test for determining the existence of a direct and immediate link” with a specific output transaction.
In reaching this conclusion, the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House also considered the previous decision of the Court of Appeal in HMRC v Associated Newspapers Limited [2017] EWCA Civ 54. Associated Newspapers incurred the cost of purchasing vouchers for retail goods which were distributed free of charge to certain purchasers of newspapers.
Although the supply of the vouchers themselves was outside the scope of VAT, it was accepted that the cost of purchasing the vouchers had a direct and immediate link with the sale of the newspapers (and also the sale of advertising space within the newspapers) so that the input VAT on the purchase of the vouchers was recoverable. Like Sveda, this was treated by the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House as an example of inputs being used for a taxpayer’s general economic activity rather than for specific transactions.
It therefore remains the case that, in determining whether a particular input transaction has a direct and immediate link with an output transaction, it is the objective use of the input which must be ascertained and not the subjective purpose of the business.
Some guidance has been given as to what constitutes (or what does not constitute) a direct and immediate link between an input transaction and an output transaction.
In Commissioners for Customs and Excise v Southern Primary Housing Limited [2003] EWCA Civ1662, the Court of Appeal made it clear at [32] that, just because an output transaction could not have taken place “but for” a particular input transaction, that did not, on its own, give rise to a sufficiently direct and immediate link and that a commercial link between an input transaction and an output transaction would also not necessarily constitute a direct and immediate link.
The Court of Appeal confirmed in Royal Opera House at [86]-[87] that the test is not one of commercial necessity.
In order for there to be a direct and immediate link between an input transaction and an output transaction, it is not necessary for the link “to be “immediate” in the sense of being close in time to the making of the output supply” (Hotel La Tour at [13]).
When considering whether there is a direct and immediate link between input transactions and output transactions, the Court of Appeal in Southern Primary emphasized at [37] that it is necessary “to look at transactions individually, component transaction by component transaction”.
Case law - apportionment
The principles set out below are applicable both to the appeals against the various assessments and the appeal against the rejection by HMRC of the 2023 PESM.
As the CJEU explained in Volkswagen Financial Services (UK) Limited v HMRC (Case C-153/17) [2019] 4 WLR 32 at [52], the objective of the apportionment exercise is “to ascertain with the greatest possible precision, the portion of VAT relating to transactions in respect of which VAT is deductible”.
If a method other than the standard turnover based method is used, it is necessary to show that “the method used guarantees as a more precise determination of the deductible proportion of the input VAT” (Volkswagen at [51]).
Having said that, this does not “mean that the method chosen must necessarily be the most precise possible” (Wolfgang und Dr Wilfried Rey Grundstücksgemeinschaft v Finanzamt Krefeld (Case C-332/14) [2017] STC 1668 at [33]).
It is fundamental that the method for apportioning input tax between taxable and exempt supplies reflects “the economic reality, assessed objectively, of the use of the relevant inputs” Hippodrome Casino Limited v HMRC [2025] EWCA Civ 1259 at [14].
When looking at the economic reality, it is legitimate to take into account “the observable terms and features of the taxpayer’s business” (HMRC v Hippodrome Casino Limited [2024] UKUT 27 (TCC) at [89] referring to the comments of Etherton LJ in HMRC v London Clubs Management [2012] STC 388 at [34]).
In Hippodrome, the Court of Appeal also observed at [64] that:
“... the standard method, established by the principal VAT directive and enshrined in domestic law, can be relied on as giving a result which is fair and reasonable (even if a bit rough and ready). It will only be displaced if the alternative proposed is more precise in its outcome.”
Ms Sloane argues that, in the case of these appeals, the standard turnover method is not the default method given that Studio had already been using a PESM since 2005 and that the requirement under regulation 102B VATR is to apportion the input tax in a way which represents the extent to which the goods or services are used in making taxable supplies.
However, given that the assessments against which Studio is appealing have been made on the basis of the standard turnover method, it is in our view right that this is, in effect, the default and that it is for Studio to show that one of its proposed alternatives gives a more accurate result.
Powers of the Tribunal – appeals against assessments/PESM
Following questions from the Tribunal, there was some discussion as to the powers of the Tribunal in relation to the appeals against the assessments on the one hand and the appeals against HMRC’s decision not to approve the 2023 PESM.
Having considered the position, the parties were agreed as to the approach which the Tribunal should follow.
As far as an appeal against HMRC's refusal to approve a PESM is concerned, the principles were set out by the Court of Session in DCM (Optical Holdings) Limited v Revenue and Customs Commissioners [2007] CSIH 58 at [16]. The key points are as follows:
The Tribunal cannot propose its own special method (St Helen’s School Northwood Limited v The Revenue and Customs Commissioners [2007] STC 633 at [27]);
A tribunal might, however, accept a proposed PESM subject to factual changes as long as this does not depart from the proposed methodology.
Where the Tribunal is invited to depart from a PESM as originally proposed, the question is therefore whether the departure changes the underlying methodology or whether it is the application of the same methodology to the correct facts as found by the Tribunal (St John’s College, Oxford v HMRC [2010] UKFTT 133 (TC) at [81] and [82]).
As confirmed by Etherton J in Banbury Visionplus Limited v HMRC [2006] STC 1568 at [44], the Tribunal has full appellate jurisdiction in respect of an appeal under s 83(e) VATA (which covers refusal to approve a PESM). This means that the Tribunal can reach its own decision as to whether the proposed PESM is more accurate than the standard turnover method. It is not confined to considering whether HMRC’s decision to reject the PESM was reasonable.
Turning to appeals against assessments, the Tribunal again has full appellate jurisdiction (the appeals being either under s 83(1)(e) VATA or s 83(1)(p) VATA). However, in this case, the objective of the Tribunal is to determine the correct amount of tax (see HMRC v General Motors (UK) Limited [2015] UKUT 605 (TCC) at [69]).
This means that, as long as it is done in a way which is procedurally fair, the Tribunal may base its decision on any method proposed by either of the parties or, indeed, on a method which is proposed by the Tribunal itself (see NHS Lothian Health Board v HMRC [2022] UKSC 28 at [76]).
The Tribunal does not, in this case, suggest that the appeals against the assessment should be determined on a basis which has not been proposed by either of the parties. The principles set out above however do make it clear that, as long as procedural fairness is observed, it is open to Studio to propose alternative methods for apportioning input tax on the residual costs between taxable and exempt supplies.
In this case, Studio proposes only two alternative methods. One is based on the 2023 PESM, subject to a proposed modification as to the assumed purchases by an average customer in a year. The Tribunal directed Studio to provide calculations showing the impact of the proposed modifications and gave HMRC the opportunity to make submissions in respect of those calculations. HMRC have provided such submissions. Although not given permission to do so, Studio subsequently provided some observations on the points made by HMRC to clarify certain aspects of the calculations. We have taken all of these points into account.
The second alternative is, as we have explained, a part of two of the three alternative methods which had previously been proposed by Studio and which HMRC had the opportunity to consider prior to the hearing.
We are therefore satisfied that both of these alternatives could provide the basis for a determination by the Tribunal in relation to the assessments should we find that they provide a more accurate apportionment of the input VAT than the standard turnover method.
Attribution of the photography and modelling costs
Analogous cases
Before summarising the parties’ submissions, it is convenient to mention a number of case law authorities referred to by the parties. We have not yet referred to most of these authorities as, for the most part, they provide examples of the applications of the principles we have referred to in paragraphs [90]-[107] above and do not establish any new principles.
As we have already explained, these authorities must be approached with some caution given the consistent message from the Courts that matters of attribution and apportionment of costs which give rise to input VAT between taxable and exempt supplies are acutely fact sensitive.
In Royal Agricultural College v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [2002] VAT Decision 17508 (a decision of the VAT and Duties Tribunal - case reference number: (LON/00/1017)), the College argued that certain advertising costs had a direct and immediate link not only with exempt supplies of education but also taxable supplies such as those made by the College’s shops and bars. The advertisements did not refer specifically to the shops and bars.
The Tribunal concluded at [40]-[43] that the objective purpose of the advertising was to attract students so as to provide them with (exempt) education. Any link between the advertising costs and the supplies made by the College bar or shop was indirect and was not immediate in the sense that it involved a subsequent step after a student had been recruited.
We have already mentioned the decision of the Court of Appeal in Dial-a-Phone which related to supplies of both exempt insurance services and taxable airtime services for mobile phones. Again, the issue was whether advertising costs had a direct and immediate link to both supplies. The advertisements in question referred both to the airtime contract and the insurance. It was decided at [72]-[73] that the objective purpose of the advertising was to promote both supplies. The advertising costs therefore had a direct and immediate link with both taxable and exempt supplies.
One point worth noting at this stage is that both Royal Agricultural College and Dial-a-Phone concern the attribution of advertising costs as a whole rather than one specific element of those advertising costs (in this case the photography and modelling costs). This is another reason for exercising caution in seeking assistance from these cases.
The Court of Appeal had to consider the attribution of input tax again in Mayflower Theatre Trust Ltd v HMRC [2006] EWCA Civ 116. The question was whether the costs of staging productions had a direct and immediate link not only with the exempt supply of tickets but also (as contended by the theatre) with taxable (or zero rated) supplies such as programmes, food and drink, sponsorship rights, corporate entertaining and advertising.
The Court of Appeal concluded at [43] that there was a direct and immediate link between the production costs and the sale of programmes because the production provided the content of the programmes. As far as food and drink was concerned, the theatre did not in fact pursue this before the Court of Appeal, although it was noted at [40] that any link between the production costs and such supplies would be indirect and not immediate (on the authority of Royal Agricultural College). Other taxable supplies including production linked merchandise and sponsorship arrangements were also found at [49] and [52] not to have a direct and immediate link with the production costs as they did not relate to a specific production.
Skipton Building Society v HMRC [2009] UKFTT 191 (TC) was a decision of this Tribunal. The issue related to input VAT on the cost of advertisements relating to properties for sale placed in local newspapers by Skipton’s estate agency business.
It was held that the costs of the advertisements which mentioned that Skipton also offered mortgage services had a direct and immediate link not only with the taxable supplies relating to the sale of the houses but also the exempt supplies connected with the mortgage services. The Tribunal Judge observed at [26] that “though ultimate aim is not the test, it seems to me that in the case of advertising what the advertiser intends to promote is likely to be the best available guide to what he is in fact promoting.”
However, relying on the decision in Royal Agricultural College, the Tribunal concluded at [27] that there was no direct and immediate link with the mortgage services if an advertisement did not “overtly mention mortgage services”.
Again, we note that the issue in Skipton related to the overall cost of advertising and not, for example, the cost of photographing the relevant properties as a separate input cost.
This Tribunal looked again at the attribution of input VAT in The Roald Dahl Museum and Story Centre v HMRC [2014] UKFTT 308 (TC). The museum incurred expenditure refurbishing and maintaining museum exhibits. It argued that this expenditure had a direct and immediate link not only with the exempt supply of tickets to the museum but also taxable supplies made by the museum shop.
The Tribunal concluded at [83]-[85] that there was no direct and immediate link between the exhibit costs and the supplies made by the shop, finding that almost all of the items in question could be (and many were) sold in any shop. An analogy was drawn with Royal Agricultural College and Mayflower. It was accepted at [90] that there was a commercial link between the exhibit costs and the supplies made by the shop (the profits from the shop subsidising the museum) but that was not sufficient.
In addition, photographs of the museum exhibits did not have a direct and immediate link with the exhibit costs, as “costs incurred in making one supply are not cost components of a second supply, merely because the practical effect of making the first supply is that it becomes feasible, or even easier, to make the second supply” (at [185]).
The only item sold in the shop which was held at [112] to have a direct and immediate link with the exhibition costs was a book which interpreted the objects in the museum and was produced in conjunction with the refurbishment of the museum. In a sense, this was similar to the decision in Mayflower where the production cost provided the content for the programmes relating to that production.
Both parties referred in some detail to the decision of this Tribunal in N Brown Group PLC v HMRC [2019] UKFTT 172 (TC). On the face of it, that appeal has some similarities with the current appeal. N Brown was a fashion retailer. Like Studio, it primarily sold goods online and by mail order, although it also had some physical shops. Customers were able to pay in cash or purchase on credit and so the business made both taxable and exempt supplies. The Tribunal had to consider both the attribution of input VAT incurred on marketing costs (including photography and modelling costs) and the apportionment of input VAT related to both taxable and exempt supplies.
The Tribunal found that N Brown had the same sort of integrated business strategy as Studio accepts exists in its case. The supply of goods supported the supply of credit and the supply of credit (through the use of a “personal account” - similar to a Studio Pay account) generated further sales.
One difference to our findings in this case is that, in the case of N Brown, it was found at [111] that, in most of the marketing materials, any references to credit were “at most tangential”. The Tribunal in N Brown accepted at [179] that input costs relating to the preparation of marketing material that contained a reference to credit had a direct and immediate link both to the taxable supplies of goods and the exempt supplies of credit.
The result of this is that the focus of the Tribunal in N Brown was on whether the costs of marketing materials which did not refer to credit nonetheless had a sufficiently direct and immediate link with the supplies of credit.
Whilst accepting at [179] that there were “strong arguments that could be made to the effect that such marketing material was not “used for” the purpose of making exempt supplies of finance”, the Tribunal nonetheless concluded at [180]-[191] that, given the integrated (two way) relationship between sales of goods and sales of credit, there was a sufficiently direct and immediate link between the marketing costs and the supplies of credit, even where the marketing materials did not refer to credit.
The Tribunal rejected the suggestion that its conclusion meant that any input cost relating to the sale of goods inevitably had a direct and immediate link to the supply of credit as well. It concluded at [193] that, although the focus is on use of the goods or services to which the input cost relates, marketing costs were used in a different way to, for example, the cost of purchasing the item for onward sale.
We should note that it is apparent from the very brief discussion of photography costs at [218] that the appellant in N Brown did not seek to distinguish between photography costs and other marketing costs in the same way as Studio does in these appeals.
As we shall see, Ms Sloane suggests that, in the light of the decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House (see further below), the Tribunal in N Brown applied the wrong test in that the integrated nature of a business cannot, of itself, give rise to a sufficiently direct and immediate link between input costs and supplies which would otherwise only have an indirect or commercial link with such supplies.
We have already referred to the decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House. The question was whether there was a direct and immediate link between the production costs of a particular production and taxable supplies of food and drink (as well as with the exempt supply of tickets). The Court drew a distinction at [46] between production costs and the costs of advertising the catering services.
The Court of Appeal concluded at [87]-[88] that, although there might be a link of commercial necessity (there would be no supplies of food or drink without the production), this was no more than a “but for” link and was not sufficient to provide a direct and immediate link between the production costs and the catering supplies.
This was despite the fact that the unchallenged evidence at [7] was that a visit to the Royal Opera House was “a fully integrated visitor experience” and at [9] that there was “a virtuous circle, whereby the high quality of the artistic output drove demand for the catering offered by the ROH, which in turn increased the income available for spending on the artistic output”.
The First-tier Tribunal returned to the question of attribution after the decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House in Sofology Limited v HMRC [2022] UKFTT 00153 (TC). The costs in question in that case were the costs of Google advertising in circumstances where Sofology supplied sofas and also services relating to insurance for the sofas. Supplies were made online, by telephone and in store.
The Tribunal at [172] rejected HMRC’s argument that the Google advertising costs had a direct and immediate link with the exempt supply of insurance services as well as the supplies of sofas despite the fact that the supplies of insurance services were found at [190] to be an important part of Sofology’s business and at [191] that there was a close economic link between the adverts and the supplies of insurance services.
In reaching this conclusion, the Tribunal placed importance at [194(1)] that the search terms for which Sofology paid did not include any reference to insurance and neither did the landing pages when a customer clicked on the relevant link. The importance the Tribunal placed in its conclusions about the content of the relevant adverts and the landing pages to which a customer was taken when clicking on the results produced by the Google advertising can be seen from the Tribunal’s comments at [196(3)-(5)].
It was also said at [194(2)] to be relevant that “insurance could be purchased only in conjunction with the purchase of a sofa, and consequent upon the user’s decision to purchase the sofa” and to be irrelevant that Sofology could predict the likely amount of income from insurance services based on the income from the sales of sofas – i.e. the relationship between the two remained relatively constant.
In addition, the Tribunal noted at [194(4)] that Sofology promoted its insurance services by other means, such as sales staff in the shops and specific marketing aimed at insurance, most of which took place after a customer had decided to purchase a sofa.
The final case we need to refer to is the decision of this Tribunal in Littlewoods which we have already mentioned. This is perhaps the most relevant to the attribution issue as it relates to photography and modelling costs in very similar circumstances to these appeals. We understand that permission has been granted for an appeal by HMRC to the Upper Tribunal which will be heard in early December.
Like Studio, Littlewoods sold a wide range of goods through catalogues and through its website. A significant proportion of purchases were made on credit. The question for the Tribunal was whether the costs of producing photographs of the products being sold had a direct and immediate link only with the taxable supply of those products or whether (as contended by HMRC) they also had a direct and immediate link with the exempt supplies of credit.
Both the catalogues and website pages contained references to flexible payment options. As in this case, there was a “symbiosis” between the sale of goods and the granting of credit, with the purchase of goods generating credit income and the availability of credit increasing sales.
The Tribunal concluded at [135] and [146] that there was no direct and immediate link between the costs of the photographs and the exempt supply of credit. It distinguished at [129] the decision in N Brown on the basis that, unlike in that case, a majority of Littlewood’s customers did not in fact incur any interest.
In any event, it did not consider at [134] that the decision in N Brown, being based on the interdependency of the supplies of goods on the one hand and the supplies of credit on the other, could stand in the light of the subsequent decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House. The fact that the sale of goods gave rise to a predictable supply of credit did not provide a direct and immediate link between the supply of credit and the photographs used to promote the goods in the same way that the production costs incurred by the Royal Opera House did not have a direct and immediate link with the supply of food and drink, even though customers who bought tickets for the production would predictably purchase and consume food and drink.
As to the objective use of the photographs, the Tribunal in Littlewoods took the view at [142] that, although messages relating to credit or flexible payment options appeared alongside the photographs, the photographs were used only to display the product. The supplies of credit were promoted by the text itself and not the photographs.
The parties’ submissions
Studio accepts that its website, catalogues, and other marketing materials promote both the sale of goods and the supply of credit. It therefore accepts that costs such as printing the catalogues and designing the website are residual costs (in the sense of having a direct and immediate link with both taxable and exempt supplies), which need to be apportioned between the taxable and exempt supplies.
However, Ms Sloane submits that it does not follow that all of the costs incurred in the creation and content of such materials are used to promote both supplies. It is necessary, she says, to look at each component transaction individually (Southern Primary at [37]).
Looking at the photography and modelling costs, Ms Sloane submits that the only objective use of the photographs which derive from those costs is to display the products. In effect, the photographs are, she says, the equivalent of a rail of dresses in a bricks-and-mortar shop. They allow the customer to inspect the goods.
As far as the supplies of credit are concerned, Ms Sloane argues that the only part of the relevant materials which promote the credit is the text itself which mentions Studio Pay, flexible payment options or makes other references to credit, and not the photographs, even though the text referring to credit may appear on the same page as the photographs or even on top of or next to the photographs.
Ms Sloane again draws an analogy with a bricks-and-mortar shop. The shop may advertise credit with signage or leaflets, but that does not, in her submission, mean that the costs of displaying the products in the shop have a direct and immediate link with the supply of credit. It is only the costs of the signage and the leaflets which have such a link.
In effect, these were the arguments which were accepted by this Tribunal in Littlewoods at [142–146].
Ms Sloane accepts that a small number of photographs (a few hundred out of a library of several hundred thousand) were, in Mr Kendrick’s words, “repurposed” by being used on leaflets primarily promoting credit but also displaying selected products. However, she says these are no different to the catalogues and the website in that the photographs only promote the products and the credit is promoted by the text.
In relation to this, Ms Sloane also notes that HMRC’s guidance in PE78200 suggests that there is only a direct and immediate link to supplies where there is a firm intention to make such supplies. On this basis, she submits that where photographs were not originally intended to be used on leaflets primarily promoting credit but were subsequently “repurposed”, there would be no direct and immediate link between the cost of producing the photographs and the exempt supplies of credit.
Ms Sloane further submits that, even if the photographs appearing on these leaflets were promoting credit, any use of the photography and modelling costs for such purposes is de minimis and should not result in any restriction on the amount of input VAT which can be recovered. She notes that, in HMRC’s guidance at PE41500, it is suggested that, where high value supplies are generated using negligible resources, the value of those supplies should be excluded from any apportionment calculation.
We pause to note that, as Mr Watkinson observed (and as is clear from the HMRC guidance Ms Sloane refers to), strictly, this is an issue which should be addressed at the apportionment stage and not the attribution stage, given that Regulation 101(2)(b) VATR refers to goods or services being used “exclusively” in making taxable supplies. There is no de minimis exception.
Assuming there is no direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the supply of credit based on the way in which the photographs are actually used, Ms Sloane submits that no such link can be established simply on the basis that Studio operates an integrated business of supplying goods on credit or that there is a symbiotic relationship between the supply of goods and the supply of credit.
Whilst there is a commercial and economic link, and whilst the supplies of credit could not take place “but for” the supplies of goods, Ms Sloane notes that it is clear from the authorities (see, for example, Royal Opera House and Sofology) that this is not sufficient.
In this context, Ms Sloane submits that the Tribunal in N Brown came to the wrong conclusion in deciding that marketing costs relating to adverts which made no reference to credit nonetheless had a direct and immediate link to supplies of credit, given the integrated, two way relationship between the supplies of goods and the supplies of credit, arguing that the decision cannot be right in the light of the decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House.
In particular, Ms Sloane argues that the fact that one of the ultimate purposes of the business is to promote credit (or catering in the case of Royal Opera House), and that this will generate a predictable income stream, does not provide a sufficiently direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the supplies of credit.
Ms Sloane suggests that, if, as a result of the integrated nature of the business, there were a sufficiently direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the supplies of credit, there is no reason why there should not also be a sufficiently direct and immediate link between other costs relating to the sale of products (such as purchase, manufacturing, storage, and distribution costs) and the supplies of credit. However, she observes that HMRC do not suggest that there is any such link.
HMRC’s position is that the objective use of the photographs is to promote credit as well as the supplies of goods, so that there is a direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs used to produce the photographs and the exempt supplies of credit.
Mr Watkinson submits that, once it is accepted that the marketing materials which use the photographs, including the catalogues and the website, promote both the goods and the credit, the costs of creating those materials (including the photography and modelling costs) inevitably have a direct and immediate link to both outputs (as was the case in Skipton and Dial-a-Phone).
Mr Watkinson makes the point that the photographs which result from the photography and modelling costs do not themselves advertise anything until they are put in some sort of context by being included in the marketing materials, such as the catalogues or the website. He submits that treating a component cost of those materials (in this case, photography and modelling) as separate from the marketing in which it was in fact used ignores the exempt use of the cost.
In any event, as far as the website is concerned, Mr Watkinson notes that the wording relating to credit appears in close proximity to the photographs and on this basis submits that the photographs are being used in relation to the supplies of credit as well as the supplies of the goods themselves.
