Even if this were not the case, Mr Watkinson argues that the integrated nature of Studio’s business model leads inevitably to the conclusion that there is a sufficiently direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the exempt supplies of credit on the basis that the objective purpose of Studio's marketing was to increase the number of customers purchasing goods through a credit account, which would, in turn, further increase sales.
Mr Watkinson submits that this goes well beyond a commercial/economic or “but for” link, and that it is legitimate to consider the objective purpose of the marketing without this falling foul of the requirement not to take into account the ultimate aim of the taxpayer. It was in this context that Mr Watkinson deployed his argument that the courts now take a broader view of the use made of a particular input which, for the reasons explained at paragraphs [97]-[102] above, we have rejected.
Based on the decision of the Court of Appeal in Dial-a-Phone, Mr Watkinson however submits that, in the case of marketing costs, when determining the objective use to which costs are put, it is necessary to consider what supplies the marketing was intended to attract customers to. In Dial-a-Phone itself, it was held that the marketing was intended to attract customers both to sign up to an airtime contract and also to take out insurance. In the same way, Mr Watkinson suggests that, in the present case, the purpose of the marketing was to encourage customers to buy products and to take out credit.
In relation to this, Mr Watkinson submits that, as recognised by the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House at [46], there is a difference between marketing costs and other costs. Marketing costs will have a direct and immediate link with the supplies which they are being used to promote. Whereas other costs (such as the production costs in Royal Opera House) may not have such a link even if the subjective intention of the business is to promote such supplies.
As noted in Sofology at [185], Mr Watkinson argues that it is permissible to take into account a business’ marketing strategy as part of the objective evidence, even though subjective purposes cannot be taken into account.
On this basis, Mr Watkinson does not accept that the decision in N Brown was wrong. If, based on the nature and strategy of the business, marketing costs are objectively used to promote two different supplies, they will have a direct and immediate link with both supplies.
Mr Watkinson argues that there is, in any event, difference between this case and N Brown. He says that, given the strategy of the business, the marketing costs in effect represent an upfront investment in acquiring customers, the result of which is to generate both supplies of goods and supplies of credit.
Discussion of attribution of photography and modelling costs
As is clear from the principles we have set out above (paragraphs [90]-[107]), we must look at all of the circumstances of the transactions, but should not take into account Studio's subjective aims. There may be a sufficiently direct and immediate link with the supplies of credit even though there is a more direct and immediate link with the supplies of goods. A commercial or economic link is not, of itself, sufficient. Nor is it enough that the supplies of credit could not take place, but for the supply of the goods.
We bear in mind that the question we have to determine is not whether marketing costs generally have a direct and immediate link with the supply of credit, but whether the photography and modelling costs specifically have a direct and immediate link with the supply of credit.
This is an important distinction and one which distinguishes this case from some of the others we have looked at such as Skipton, Dial-a-Phone and Sofology. In our view, it also distinguishes this case from N Brown as, although the Tribunal in that case looked at a long list of marketing expenses, including photography expenses, no distinction was made in the decision between the different types of expense. There is no evidence that any special case was made in relation to the photography expenses compared to any of the other expenses.
As we have noted, it is accepted by Studio that the catalogues, website and other marketing materials which use the photographs promote both the supply of goods and the supply of credit and that, in general, costs incurred in producing these materials are objectively used for the purposes of both supplies. This is entirely consistent with authorities such as Royal Agricultural College, Dial-a-Phone, Skipton and Sofology given the references to the availability of credit contained in those materials.
We do, however, accept that each component transaction must be considered separately (Southern Primary at [37]) and that it is therefore necessary to consider the objective use to which the photographs contained in those materials are put. It does not automatically follow that just because the photography and modelling costs are a cost component of the marketing materials, the photographs which result from those costs are being used for the purposes of the supply of credit.
Having said that, taking into account all the facts and circumstances relating to the transactions, we have reached the conclusion that there is a sufficiently direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the exempt supplies of credit based on the way in which the photographs are used in the marketing materials.
We agree that the primary function of the photographs in the catalogues and on the website is to help describe the products to potential customers. However, we accept Mr Watkinson's submission that, in order to have any meaning, the photographs must be placed into some sort of context. A catalogue or website which contained the pictures but nothing else would be unlikely to achieve any sales.
In this case, the context includes the other information and content contained in the catalogues, website and other marketing materials. This includes, for example, a written description of the products, the price and, in some cases, the availability of credit.
As we have seen, although some of the messages relating to credit are generic, for example, the banners that appear at the top of every webpage, there are other messages which are specific to particular products.
In the catalogues, these include the branded “Studio Pay” wording, which is superimposed on the photographs of certain products, particularly (and deliberately) higher value items. As far as the website is concerned, we were provided with a number of examples of web pages relating to specific products with prominent wording relating to the availability of credit alongside the photograph where the price of the product is shown. The wording relating to credit is significantly more prominent than the actual description of the product, as well as being closer to the photograph of the product.
In the light of this, it is in our view artificial to suggest that the only part of the catalogues and the website which promote credit is the text which refers to the credit and not the photographs as well.
We accept that it is possible to have marketing materials which promote two separate supplies and for photographs included in those marketing materials to have a direct and immediate link with one supply but not the other.
Ms Sloane gave as an example of this, an M&S brochure marketing both its food products and its clothing products. Photographs of the food would not have a direct and immediate link with the supply of clothes and vice versa.
However, that is very different to the present situation where the catalogues and the website have a photograph of a specific product with prominent wording encouraging a customer to purchase that specific product on credit. Objectively, the photograph is, in our view, being used in relation to the supply of credit as well as the supply of the product itself. This is because the wording relating to credit which is aimed at the specific product can only properly be understood and assessed when taken together with the other details of the product, including its description (of which the photographs form part) and the price.
We can see some force in Ms Sloane's analogy with a bricks-and-mortar shop. The photographs in the catalogues and website could be seen as the equivalent of the physical display of the goods in the shop and the messages relating to credit could be seen as the equivalent of separate signage or leaflets dotted around the shop. In such circumstances, it is unlikely that the cost of displaying the products in the shop would have a direct and immediate link to the supply of credit.
We are not, however, convinced that it is possible to draw a direct analogy between the sale of goods by mail order or online on the one hand and the sale of goods in a physical shop on the other. It is a completely different business model, no doubt with different drivers as to the way in which the products are marketed to potential customers.
One difference, for example, is that, on the website, messages relating to credit and flexible payment appear on every product page. Whilst it might in theory be possible for a physical shop to place messages referring to credit next to every product it sells, we suspect that this would be unusual. As submitted by Mr Watkinson, if this were to happen, it might well be the case that the costs of displaying the goods might have a direct and immediate link to supplies of credit.
We appreciate that our conclusion on this issue is different to the conclusion reached by the Tribunal in Littlewoods. It may be that this can be explained by differences in the facts. For example, in Littlewoods it is said at [142] that the information about credit was “provided discreetly alongside the photographs”, whereas, in the case of Studio there was nothing discreet about the messages relating to credit and some of them were superimposed on the photographs themselves. As the Tribunal itself noted in Littlewoods at [129], even small factual differences can change the result.
We are also of the view that the photographs of products contained in the leaflets which are primarily designed to market credit have a direct and immediate link with the supplies of credit. It is hard to see how a different conclusion could be reached. Alongside the photographs is the name of the product and the price, but there is no separate description of the product as would be found in the catalogues or the website. The main focus of the leaflets is various messages about credit. There can be no doubt that the photographs are being used for the purposes of supplies of credit.
It is no doubt for this reason that Ms Sloane picked up on Mr Kendrick's suggestion in his evidence that when used in the context of these leaflets, the photographs were being “repurposed”.
However, we do not accept this description. It is clear from the evidence that the leaflets primarily aimed at promoting credit were a regular feature of Studio's marketing. It is also clear from the evidence that the leaflets typically contain photographs of products alongside the name and the price of the product.
We infer from this that the business always knew and intended that some of the photographs would be used in this way. Even when used as part of a leaflet primarily promoting credit, the photographs are also being used to encourage customers to purchase the products themselves as well as to pay on credit.
Whilst it may be the case that a decision as to which photographs would appear in the credit leaflets was only taken sometime subsequently, we do not consider that this means that it can be said that the photography and modelling costs were not intended to be used for the purposes of the exempt supplies of credit at the time they were incurred.
We have considered the other cases which the parties have referred to and which we have briefly summarised but have not found these particularly helpful by way of analogy given that, with the exception of Littlewoods, the factual background is very different.
We accept Mr Kendrick's evidence that only around five per cent of the pages of the catalogue referred to credit in the way that we have described. We also acknowledge that we have no direct evidence as to the number of individual product pages on the website which contain the prominent messages relating to credit in relation to that specific product.
We were however provided with a number of examples of individual product pages, more of which contained such wording than did not. We infer from this that it was certainly not unusual for references to credit in relation to a particular product to appear alongside that product on the website.
Based on the evidence we have available, we do not consider that the use of the photography and modelling costs for the purposes of the supplies of credit can be said to be de minimis (even if that were relevant at the attribution stage) given that it includes the costs relating to all of the photographs in the catalogues on which the Studio Pay wording is superimposed, all of the photographs on the individual product pages of the website which contain prominent messages relating to credit alongside the price of that particular product, as well as the photographs used in the leaflets primarily promoting credit.
In making this finding, we are conscious that, at the attribution stage, the question is, in any event, whether the costs are attributable exclusively to taxable supplies. Indeed, in her opening submissions, Ms Sloane accepted that, if only one photograph was used for the purposes of the supplies of credit, the entirety of the photography and modelling costs would be “residual costs”, which would need to be dealt with at the apportionment stage (a similar result to that in the Roald Dahl Museum case, where use of the exhibition costs in respect of a taxable supply of a single product in the shop meant that the entirety of the exhibition costs could then be apportioned between exempt and taxable supplies).
Given our conclusion that, based on the context in which the photographs are placed in the catalogues, the website and the credit leaflets, the photography and modelling costs are, objectively, used for the purposes of Studio's supplies of credit (as well as the supply of goods), we do not strictly need to deal with HMRC's separate argument that, if this were found not to be the case, the photography and modelling costs are, in any event, used for the purposes of the exempt supplies of credit as a result of the integrated and symbiotic nature of Studio's business. However, as this was fully argued, we will address the point briefly.
Mr Watkinson's key submission is that, when considering whether marketing costs have a direct and immediate link to a particular supply, it is necessary to ask what, objectively, the marketing materials in question aim to promote. As mentioned above, in support of this, he refers to the decision of the Court of Appeal in Dial-a-Phone.
Whilst it is true that the Court of Appeal accepted the finding of the First-tier Tribunal that the adverts in question were intended to attract customers both to sign up to an airtime contract and to take out mobile phone insurance, the reason for this was that the adverts referred specifically to insurance and was not based on any integrated or symbiotic business strategy.
Mr Watkinson seeks to extend this principle so that marketing costs will have a direct and immediate link to a particular supply even where the marketing materials do not make any reference to that supply if there is a sufficiently integrated business model from which it can be concluded that the purpose of the marketing material was to promote such supplies. This was the approach taken by the Tribunal in N Brown.
Mr Watkinson accepts that the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House concluded that, in the case of production costs an integrated business strategy was insufficient to give rise to a direct and immediate link between those production costs and supplies of catering services. However, he submits that, as recognised by the Court of Appeal at [46], the position is different in relation to marketing costs.
We do not accept this. What the Court of Appeal referred to in that paragraph was the contrast between the production costs on the one hand and, by way of example, costs incurred in advertising the catering services. Clearly, costs of specific adverts for the catering services would have a direct and immediate link with the supplies of catering.
What the Court of Appeal did not say is that the cost of advertising a particular production would have a direct and immediate link with the catering supplies as a result of the integrated nature of the Royal Opera House's business model even if the advert did not mention catering services.
There is therefore no reason to suppose that the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House would have come to any different conclusion had the costs in question been marketing costs relating to a particular production (which did not mention the catering services) as opposed to production costs. Indeed, there is every reason to think that the Court of Appeal would have come to the same conclusion.
Mr Watkinson relied heavily on the decision of the Court of Appeal in Associated Newspapers in suggesting that a broader analysis of the use of particular costs should be undertaken when considering how those costs had been used by the business. However, as we have explained, the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House rejected at [83] a similar submission, as did the Supreme Court in Hotel La Tour at [95]–[96] (although the discussion there focussed on a very different set of circumstances).
Based on what was said in those cases, we agree that there is no broader test for establishing a direct and immediate link between input costs and specific supplies (as opposed to establishing a link with the taxpayer’s business as a whole in circumstances where the transaction with which the inputs have the closest link is outside the scope of VAT).
Like the Tribunal in Littlewoods, we think it unlikely that the Tribunal in N Brown would have reached the same conclusion had the decision of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House been available to it.
The decision in N Brown was predicated on the two-way (or symbiotic) relationship between sales of goods and supplies of credit. However, the fact that the strategy of the business in N Brown was to encourage customers to take credit and that the sale of goods would lead to a predictable supply of credit is, in our view, no more than a “but for”, commercial or economic link between the two supplies. It focuses (impermissibly) on the ultimate aim of the taxpayer and not the objective use to which the marketing costs are put.
In reaching this conclusion, we recognise that the strategy of the business may be an objective feature of a business which it is relevant to take into account (Sofology at [185] and London Clubs Management at [34]). However, in our view, this is not sufficient to elevate a “but for” or commercial link to a direct and immediate link. Any such conclusion would, as we have said, be placing too much weight on the ultimate aim of the taxpayer, in circumstances where the marketing materials in question make no mention of the exempt supplies of credit.
The conclusion that the integrated or symbiotic nature of the supplies made by a business cannot, of itself, determine whether (objectively) there is a direct and immediate link between marketing costs and supplies that are not mentioned in the marketing materials is consistent with previous authorities including, for example, Royal Agricultural College, Skipton, Dial-a-Phone, and Sofology. It is also consistent with previous cases dealing with other categories of costs such as Mayflower and Roald Dahl Museum. More importantly, it is consistent with the reasoning of the Court of Appeal in Royal Opera House.
Had the photographs not in fact been used for the purposes of the supplies of credit in the relevant marketing materials, we would therefore have concluded that there was no direct and immediate link between the photography and modelling costs and the supplies of credit simply as a result of the (admitted) integrated and symbiotic nature of Studio's business.
We cannot see that any different conclusion would be reached if the point is put on the basis that the marketing costs represent an upfront investment in acquiring a customer. This is simply another way of saying that the ultimate aim of the business is for customers both to purchase goods and to incur credit interest. For the reasons we have already explained, it does not lead to the conclusion that the photography and modelling costs have a direct and immediate link with the supply of credit as well as the supply of goods.
Having decided that the photography and modelling costs form part of the residual marketing costs, we turn now to consider the apportionment of those costs between taxable and exempt supplies.
Apportionment
The parties' submissions
We deal here with the appeals against the various assessments made by HMRC to the extent that those assessments relate to the apportionment of residual costs (i.e. those costs which do not relate exclusively to taxable supplies or to exempt supplies) between exempt and taxable supplies. As we have already mentioned, those assessments were made on the basis that the residual costs should be apportioned using the standard turnover method.
Studio now only takes issue with this in relation to marketing costs. It is accepted that all other residual costs should be apportioned using the standard turnover method. As a result of our conclusion in relation to the attribution issue, the marketing costs include the photography and modelling costs.
We should note that Studio has not made any separate proposals to adjust the apportionment of photography and modelling costs. Those costs therefore fall to be apportioned in the same way as all other marketing costs.
As we have already explained at paragraphs [108]-[116], the search is for a method which objectively reflects the use of the costs and it is for Studio to show that one or other of their alternatives guarantees is a more precise determination of the deductible proportion of the input VAT than the standard turnover method, in each case, taking into account the economic reality of the use of the relevant inputs. In assessing economic reality, account should be taken of the “observable terms and features of the taxpayer’s business” (London Clubs Management at [34]).
Studio says that using the standard turnover method in relation to marketing costs produces distortions and that, as a result, their proposed alternative methods produce a result which is more precise and which is fairer and more reasonable.
Whilst Studio accepts that the marketing costs have a direct and immediate link with supplies of credit as well as supplies of goods (and therefore need to be apportioned as residual costs), it does not accept that marketing costs incurred in year one continue to have a direct and immediate link with all payments of interest (including those received in future years) which relate to products purchased in year one.
It is important to note in this context that it is common ground that the effect of regulation 90(1)(a) VATR is that each payment of interest represents a separate supply of credit and so it is necessary to consider what costs incurred by Studio are used for the purposes of each of those subsequent supplies of credit.
In essence, Studio’s submission is based on the underlying proposition that any link between the marketing materials which induce a customer to purchase goods and, as a result, to incur credit interest, decays over time and that there comes a point when it cannot be said that the costs of those marketing materials are in any sense used for the purposes of the later supplies of credit represented by those payments of interest. This follows the reasoning of the Tribunal in N Brown at [196] and [234]–[237].
In N Brown, the parties were given an opportunity to consider these observations of the Tribunal. It is understood that a settlement was reached and that there was no need for the parties to return to the Tribunal for a determination of the correct method of apportionment.
It is this perceived distortion which Studio took into account when making the adjustments required in response to the special method override notice issued by HMRC in 2018. It did this by excluding an estimated amount of interest said to represent interest received more than 12 months after a particular sale.
However, following the evidence at the Tribunal hearing, Studio now accepts that it has no reliable way of tracking interest paid back to a particular sale. As a result, it has abandoned any alternative methods based on excluding from the apportionment calculation all or part of the amount of interest received more than a specified period after a sale has taken place as it is impossible for it to calculate the amount of such interest.
In order to address what it considers to be the distortions created by the standard turnover method, Studio now proposes two alternatives:
The first is based on the 2023 PESM proposal which was rejected by HMRC. This seeks to calculate (based on a number of assumptions) the total amount of interest expected to be generated at any time in the future from purchases made by an average credit account customer in the year in which the apportionment calculation is taking place and to include only such interest in the apportionment calculation rather than the actual interest received in the relevant period.
In his oral evidence, Mr Jones identified an error in the calculations contained in the 2023 PESM. The model had assumed a single purchase of £75 by a customer during the year. This is the average amount of an order placed by a customer purchasing on credit. However, Studio’s analysis shows that a credit customer will place between three and four orders each year and that the total spend during a year for a customer purchasing on credit is £250.
Studio has therefore put forward two updated models for the 2023 PESM. One is based on a single purchase at the start of the year of £250. The other assumes three purchases of £75 each in months one, five, and nine of the financial year. This would represent purchases in April, August and December as, during the period in question, Studio generally made its accounts up to a date in the last week of March each year.
The first version of this proposal, involving a single purchase of £250, results in irrecoverable VAT of approximately £2.4 million for the 2021 financial year (compared to £2.7 million based on HMRC’s standard turnover method). The second version (three purchases of £75 each) results in irrecoverable VAT of approximately £2.3 million for the 2021 year.
The second proposal put forward by Studio is to exclude from the apportionment calculation any interest paid during the period for which the apportionment is being made by a customer who, at the time the interest is paid, is in a “non-trading position”.
As previously explained, this is a customer who has failed to make the minimum monthly payment and, as a result, no longer receives any marketing materials and is unable to place any further orders until the default has been remedied.
This method would result in irrecoverable VAT in the 2021 financial year of approximately £2.5 million.
Underlying both these proposals is a submission that marketing materials are, objectively, only being used by the business to generate the interest income which Studio anticipated would be received from an average customer at the time a purchase was made. The first proposal reflects this by only including interest which would be paid by an average customer making average monthly repayments. The second proposal excludes interest which would not be expected due to a customer being in default.
Ms Sloane argues that the marketing materials cannot be said to be used in any meaningful way to generate interest above and beyond this. Instead, she suggests that such interest (or the decision to continue to incur interest) is likely to be the product of external events such as (by way of example) COVID or changes to the customer’s employment status.
In support of this, Ms Sloane makes the point that, under Financial Conduct Authority rules, Studio cannot use marketing materials to encourage customers to continue to pay interest, to go into default or to incur default interest. She notes that the evidence shows that Studio tightened up its acceptance criteria for credit accounts in order to minimise potential defaults. In addition, it set its minimum payments at a higher level than some of its competitors with the specific purpose of trying to ensure that balances were paid off quicker and that customers did not therefore fall into default.
Ms Sloane adds that it was clearly not in Studio’s interests for customers to go into default, given that such customers could not make further purchases.
As Ms Sloane observes, customers who do go into default end up paying significantly more interest as they have a larger unpaid balance and are paying interest on the unpaid interest which has been added to their accounts. All of this can add up to significant additional costs given the high rates of interest charged. Ms Sloane argues that it was no part of Studio’s purpose when incurring the marketing costs to generate such additional interest income.
Ms Sloane cautions that it is important to distinguish between use and causation. Although she accepts that it can in some sense be said that marketing costs are the original cause of interest income being received, it does not follow that the marketing costs continue to be used in relation to future supplies of credit represented by interest income.
Ms Sloane also raises an issue relating to the timing of costs being incurred and supplies being made. She points out that the turnover basis assumes that all inputs are being used on a rolling basis in relation to supplies of credit which are made in the same period. However, this is clearly not the case whilst a customer is in default as such customers receive no marketing materials whilst they are in default. The standard turnover basis cannot therefore, she submits, provide a fair and reasonable apportionment.
HMRC, on the other hand, do not accept that the standard turnover method produces any distortion. On the contrary, Mr Watkinson draws attention to the fact that the result of using a method based in some way on expected income results in around £20m-£30m of actual interest income received in the 2021 financial year being excluded from the apportionment calculations.
Mr Watkinson points out that there is no authority for the “erosion over time” argument relied on by Studio other than the decision of this Tribunal in N Brown and, as a result, does not accept that there is any such principle.
As far as the possibility of external events influencing the payment of credit interest is concerned, Mr Watkinson observes that the right to deduct is forward looking and must be assessed at the time the relevant costs are incurred.
In relation to this, he relies on the decision of the CJEU in Belgium v Ghent Coal Terminal NV (Case C-37/95) [1998] STC 394. The circumstances of that case were rather different in that the issue related to expenditure which was intended to be used for a taxable supply but where (as a result of the land in question being sold) the supply never took place. The CJEU explained at [19]–[20] that:
“The right to deduct, once it has arisen, remains acquired even if the planned economic activity has not given rise to taxable transactions.
Likewise, the right to deduct remains acquired where the taxable person has been unable to use the goods or services which have given rise to a deduction in the context of taxable transactions by reason of circumstances beyond his control.”
The principle which Mr Watkinson derives from this decision is that, once it is established that costs are (objectively) intended to be used for future supplies, the fact that there is some intervening event or that the supplies do not take place does not prevent the costs in question from having a direct and immediate link with the supplies in question.
In any event, Mr Watkinson argues that the subjective reason why a customer pays interest is irrelevant in the context of an objective analysis as to whether residual costs are used for the purposes of the exempt supplies of credit.
Looking at the economic reality, Mr Watkinson submits that, where a customer purchases goods on credit, all of the marketing costs up to that point are used for the purposes of the future supplies of credit which relate to the purchase in question so that it is right for the apportionment calculation to take into account all of the interest in fact received rather than some artificial estimate of the expected interest.
Mr Watkinson acknowledges that calculating an apportionment based on income from retail sales and interest income in the same accounting period creates a mismatch in the sense that some of the interest received is likely to relate to sales in a previous accounting period. However, he submits that this is simply a feature of the VAT system.
In particular, Mr Watkinson notes that it is clear that input tax is deductible when the costs are incurred, irrespective of when the future taxable supply will take place (Hotel La Tour at [13]). Similarly, income from subsequent taxable supplies is taken into account in the period in which it is received even though the inputs which are cost components of those supplies may have been accounted for in some prior VAT period.
HMRC in any event do not consider that either of the alternative apportionment proposals put forward by Studio provide a fair and reasonable or more precise result than the standard turnover method.
As far as the amended 2023 PESM is concerned, HMRC contend that there is no basis for using an artificial estimate of anticipated interest in calculating the apportionment rather than using the actual interest received as, in their view, using an estimated figure does not measure or reflect the actual use of the residual marketing costs.
With respect to the second alternative method, which excludes interest paid by non-trading customers, Mr Watkinson submits that there is no basis for excluding interest paid during this period if it is accepted that marketing costs continue to be used for the purposes of all future supplies of credit relating to a specific purchase.
In any event, as mentioned above, HMRC do not accept the “erosion over time” argument to the extent that this provides the underlying basis for this method of apportionment. Mr Watkinson argues that there is no justification for excluding interest just because a customer has gone into default.
Discussion – apportionment of residual costs
Having considered all the circumstances, our conclusion is that the standard turnover method, whilst not perfect, does not lead to any significant distortion and so produces a fair and reasonable result. We do not consider that either of the alternatives proposed by Studio gives rise to a more precise apportionment of the residual marketing costs between the taxable and exempt supplies.
A significant difficulty with the case put forward by Studio has resulted from its need to accept, following oral evidence, that it could no longer put forward any alternatives which depend on excluding from any apportionment calculation all or part of the interest resulting from a particular sale, based on the length of time after the sale the interest is paid, due to its inability to identify such income reliably.
The result of this is that even if it were right that there comes a point when marketing costs are no longer used for the purposes of future supplies of credit where interest is paid many months after the supply of the goods to which the interest relates, the solutions put forward by Studio do not address that problem.
This can be seen from the fact that the first alternative (based on expected interest) contains no temporal cut-off. It purports to take account of all interest generated by a particular sale but does so on the basis of estimates and assumptions rather than based on the actual interest received.
Similarly, the second proposal does not restrict the amount of exempt interest based on any particular timescale. A customer could go into default in the second month after the purchase or at any subsequent time. On the basis of the proposal put forward by Studio, once the customer ceases to be in default (by paying off any arrears), any interest subsequently paid would still be included in the apportionment calculation however long after the purchase the interest is paid.
It is therefore hard to see how the alternative proposals can guarantee a more precise result in circumstances where they do not address the primary reason put forward as to why the standard turnover basis is not fair and reasonable.
Leaving this on one side for a moment, it appears that the principle which underpins both alternative methods proposed by Studio is that it is only interest which the business expects or intends to generate which should be included in the apportionment calculation.
Although we accept that we should take into account the “observable terms and features of the taxpayer’s business” (see paragraph [240] above), in our view, the approach which is proposed by Studio strays into the impermissible territory of taking into account Studio’s subjective motives (or “ultimate aim” as it was put in BLP).
Ms Sloane placed great emphasis on the terms of the credit agreement between Studio and its customers. She notes that this contains minimum payment terms and warnings about incurring additional interest if there is a default. However, in our view, the only objectively observable feature of this is that Studio will be entitled to receive all of the interest which is due under the terms of the credit agreement, whether or not the customer is in default and however long it happens to take a particular customer to repay their debt.
We fully accept, based on the evidence, that Studio would prefer customers not to default and that it took steps such as imposing the minimum payment terms and tightening its credit acceptance criteria to try and ensure that this was the case. It also made commercial sense for Studio to try and prevent customers from being in default as they would not then be able to place further orders. However, this seems to us to be no more than the subjective intention of the business and does not determine how the marketing costs have (objectively) been used.
Importantly, we fail to see how this intention or aim of the business leads to the conclusion that marketing costs which are accepted as being used for the purposes of exempt supplies of credit both before and after any default takes place cease to be so used during the period of any default.
It is true that the cost of the materials which are not sent to customers in default are not being used for supplies of credit which take place during the period of default. However, that does not mean the marketing costs incurred before the period of default are not so used.
Similarly, the first alternative method which seeks only to take account of interest which is expected to be paid by an average customer in our view ignores the observable terms and features of the business as it substitutes an estimated figure based on averages and assumptions for the interest which is actually received and which reflects what is due under the credit agreement.
To the extent that either of the proposed alternatives is in fact intended to address the perceived distortion caused by an erosion of any link between marketing costs and the payment of interest based on the time which has elapsed between the date when the goods were purchased and the date when interest relating to those purchases is paid, we take a different view of this than the Tribunal in N Brown. In effect, we accept Mr Watkinson’s submissions.
Looking at the economic reality, if marketing costs which are accepted as having a direct and immediate link with both the supply of goods and the supply of credit result in a purchase, we cannot see why the last payment of interest in relation to that purchase does not (objectively) use those marketing costs in exactly the same way as the first payment of interest.
As noted by Mr Watkinson, the subjective motivation of a customer which may result in them going into default or taking longer to pay off the full balance than the average customer plays no part in an objective determination as to whether input costs are used for the purposes of a particular supply.
The fact that a customer may, for example, lose their job and be unable to continue to meet the minimum payments or be able only to make the minimum payment and not to pay off 12% of the balance on their account each month (which the evidence shows is the amount paid off each month by an average customer) is simply not relevant. Looked at objectively, the marketing costs leading to the sale are intended to be used in respect of all of the supplies of credit representing the interest paid in respect of that sale, irrespective of the subjective reason why the customer chooses to pay interest.
As submitted by Mr Watkinson, this is not a “but for” (or causation) analysis. We are not saying that the future payments of interest would not have been made but for the sale so that the marketing costs which are used for the purposes of the sale are also being used for the supplies of credit. What we are saying (in agreement with the submission made by Mr Watkinson) is that marketing costs which are objectively used both for the purposes of the sale and the initial supply of credit (as is accepted), continue to be used in the same way for all subsequent supplies of credit relating to that particular sale.
We accept that this gives rise to a timing mismatch as marketing costs incurred in year one will continue to be used in respect of supplies of credit which may be made in year two or year three (or subsequently). Similarly, supplies of credit in year two or year three may not use any of the marketing costs incurred in that year (for example, because a customer is in default and is not receiving any of those marketing materials).
However, as was noted by Mr Watkinson in his skeleton argument, the proportion of credit interest as a percentage of total revenues has stayed fairly constant during the period in question. In each of the five years from 2018 to 2022 it was either 23% or 24% of total revenues, with the exception of 2021, where it was 20%.
Based on this, we do not therefore consider that any mismatch between the time when marketing costs are incurred and the time when interest is received would, over the relevant period, result in a significant distortion as a result of using the standard turnover method. The actual interest received in the year serves as a reasonable proxy for the interest generated by the sales in the relevant year, even though some of that interest may be received in later years.
We acknowledge that a similar argument was rejected by the Tribunal in N Brown at [235]–[236]. However, that was on the basis that, in contrast to our conclusions in this case, the Tribunal considered that there comes a point when the marketing costs are no longer used for the purposes of the supplies of credit represented by interest paid some years after the purchase of the goods in question.
We note that, if Studio’s first proposal were accepted, the amount of “expected” interest which would be taken into account in 2021 would only be approximately 13%-14.6% of total revenues for that year, a figure which is clearly out of line with the figures mentioned in paragraph [288] above. In the light of this, we cannot accept that this method produces a fair and reasonable result.
Studio did not provide details of the amount of interest which would be excluded if its second proposed alternative (excluding interest paid by non-trading customers) were adopted.
As Ms Sloane pointed out, the search is not for perfection. However, we consider that the standard turnover method provides a more precise apportionment than the proposed alternatives which, in carrying out the apportionment calculations, seek to ignore a significant proportion of the interest actually received which, as we have found, continues to have a direct and immediate link with the residual marketing costs (albeit, in some cases, costs incurred in a prior period).
We therefore dismiss the appeal against the assessments to the extent that the appeals relate to the apportionment of input VAT in respect of residual costs between taxable and exempt supplies on the basis of the standard turnover method.
2023 PESM
Studio appeals against HMRC’s rejection of the 2023 PESM and asks the Tribunal to allow the appeal on the basis of an amended 2023 PESM as described at paragraph [248(1)] above.
We accept that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to approve the 2023 PESM on the basis of such amendments. In our view, they do not change the methodology applied to the originally proposed 2023 PESM. They simply change the factual inputs to reflect the undisputed evidence as to the average purchases made by a customer with a credit account in any given year.
However, as will be apparent from what we have said about the appeals against the assessments, we do not accept that the 2023 PESM (as amended) guarantees a more precise apportionment of the input VAT between taxable and exempt supplies than the standard turnover method.
The appeal against the 2023 PESM is therefore dismissed.
Out of time assessments
The two assessments which are said to be out of time are an assessment which relates to the 09/19 VAT period which was issued on 1 October 2021 and an assessment which relates to the 03/20 VAT period which was made on 30 March 2022.
The assessments were made under s 73 VATA. In accordance with s 73(6) VATA the assessment cannot be made after the later of:
“(a) two years after the end of the prescribed accounting period; or
(b) one year after evidence of the facts, sufficient in the opinion of the Commissioners to justify the making of the assessment, comes to their knowledge.”
It is common ground that the assessments were not made within the two year time limit in s 73(6)(a). In the case of the assessment for the 03/20 VAT period that is because the VAT period ended on 27 March 2020 and not 31 March 2020. The focus is therefore on the alternative time limit in s 73(6)(b) VATA.
The Supreme Court in DCM (Optical Holdings) Limited v HMRC [2022] UKSC 26 confirmed the approach which should be taken by the Tribunal, approving at [18] the following statement of Dyson J in Pegasus Birds Limited v Customs and Excise Commissioners [1999] STC 95 (paragraph 4 on pages 101-102) that:
“The correct approach for a Tribunal to adopt is (i) to decide what were the facts which, in the opinion of the officer making the assessment on behalf of the Commissioners, justified the making of the assessment, and (ii) to determine when the last piece of evidence of these facts of sufficient weight to justify making the assessment was communicated to the Commissioners. The period of one year runs from the date in (ii).”
As noted by the Supreme Court in DCM at [20]:
The focus is on “the assessment which HMRC has in fact made and not a hypothetical assessment which they might have made but did not”; and
“The focus is also on the subjective opinion of the relevant HMRC official, which is a question of fact. Absent a perverse view, akin to Wednesbury unreasonableness, on the part of the official as to the adequacy of the evidence before him or her in relation to the assessment which is later made, it is HMRC's knowledge of the evidence relevant to the particular assessment which starts the clock running under s 73(6)(b).”
As to requests by HMRC for further information before making an assessment, the parties both accept the comment made by this Tribunal in Carbondesk Group Plc v HMRC [2015] UKFTT 367 (TC) at [21] that:
“…if the further investigations produce nothing of material significance the result must be that the last such piece of evidence was received before the officer asked for the further information.”
The question therefore is what evidence the HMRC officer who made the assessment in fact relied on as justifying the assessment and not when the last request for information was made (or response to such request was received) if this did not produce any further evidence which was relied on by the relevant HMRC officer.
In relation to the assessment for the 09/19 VAT period which was issued on 30 October 2021, Ms Sloane submits on behalf of Studio that HMRC had everything they needed when Studio provided the calculations for their apportionment calculations on 11 December 2019. She suggests that HMRC themselves acknowledge in their statement of case that the calculations needed were not complex given that they would just be applying the standard turnover method to the turnover figures shown in the 11 December 2019 calculations.
HMRC’s case however is that, whilst this made it clear that part of the exempt interest income had been excluded from the apportionment calculation, it did not explain the reason for this or how the amount which had been excluded had been calculated.
There is no dispute that the fact that Studio's calculations excluded any interest which it calculated had been received more than 12 months after the relevant purchase was only revealed in a letter to HMRC from Studio's accountants, PwC dated 2 November 2020. That letter did not however explain why interest charged more than 12 months after the original sale had been excluded. This was only explained by PwC in a further letter to HMRC dated 30 April 2021.
As noted by Ms Sloane, neither of the officers who made the assessments on 1 October 2021 and 30 March 2022 have given any evidence. As such, she submits that the Tribunal cannot be satisfied as to the evidence which the officers in question considered sufficient to justify the assessments.
Mr Watkinson on the other hand invites the Tribunal to infer what the subjective opinions of the assessing officers were based on the evidence provided by HMRC's witness, Mr Williamson.
In his evidence, Mr Williamson explained that the officers who made the assessments were part of HMRC's Large Business group. They were not specialists in VAT or partial exemption calculations. Mr Williamson on the other hand is a partial exemption specialist.
Mr Williamson joined the case team dealing with Studio in June 2020. At that time, he reviewed all of the information which had been provided to HMRC and drafted a letter for the Large Business Team to send to Studio asking for further information. This was sent on 17 September 2020 by the officer who issued the 1 October 2021 assessment (Paul Hughes). It is this letter which prompted PwC’s letter to HMRC dated 2 November 2020 which, for the first time, explained that interest income received more than 12 months after a purchase had been excluded for the purposes of the apportionment calculations.
Mr Williamson further explained that, when decisions relating to assessments concerning partial exemption were made, he was part of the decision making process. His evidence was that he was the person who “dictated how the case progressed” including determining whether HMRC had sufficient information (as demonstrated by the fact that he had drafted the letter dated 17 September 2020 requesting significant amounts of further information).
It is fair to note that Mr Williamson accepted on a number of occasions whilst giving evidence that he could not speak for the assessing officers as to what their opinion was at the time the assessments were issued. However, based on Mr Williamson’s evidence about his role in the decision making process, we consider that it is reasonable to infer that the assessing officers had the same opinion as Mr Williamson himself.
It is clear from Mr Williamson’s evidence that he was the person who decided what information was needed and whether an assessment was justified. As far as partial exemption was concerned, there can be little doubt that the assessing officers deferred to Mr Williamson.
Mr Williamson confirmed that he had regular discussions with the assessing officers and so they would have been up to speed with his views. As non-specialists, there is no reason to suppose that their opinions as to whether they had sufficient evidence of the facts to justify an assessment would have been any different from Mr Williamson's opinion.
Returning to the assessment issued on 1 October 2021, we accept that in December 2019, HMRC knew that some of the exempt interest income had been excluded from the partial exemption calculations. It was however, in our view, perfectly reasonable for HMRC to want to know how the amount which had been excluded had been calculated. It is clear that Mr Williamson did not consider that HMRC had sufficient information to justify an assessment without knowing what lay behind Studio's calculations. As we have said, we infer that the assessing officer, Mr Hughes, shared Mr Williamson's opinion.
As the assessment was made within 12 months of the information being provided on 2 November 2020, it was made within the time limit set out in s 73(6)(b) VATA.
We note that it is HMRC's case that the assessing officer also needed to understand the reasons for the 12 month cut off in relation to exempt interest income before making an assessment. Ms Sloane challenges this on the basis that, Mr Hughes, in a letter dated 11 March 2021 stated that HMRC “do not agree that any of the exempt income should be left out of the calculation”. However, at the end of that letter, he indicated that he would give Studio an opportunity to respond to HMRC’s concerns.
This resulted in PwC’s letter of 30 April 2021 which, amongst other things, explained the rationale for the 12 month restriction. Mr Williamson’s response to this in cross-examination was that, in order to form a view, HMRC needed to understand why the interest paid after 12 months had been excluded. We infer from this that the view expressed in the HMRC letter dated 11 March 2021 was a provisional view and that they were open to receiving additional information which might change that view.
Again, we think that this is perfectly reasonable (and indeed sensible). It is possible that the explanation might have persuaded HMRC that a restriction on the amount of interest income based on the time elapsed after the purchase of the goods in question was justified. This explanation was part of the evidence taken into account by HMRC in making the assessment. It is not a situation where further information was requested but nothing new was received.
Another piece of information referred to by Mr Williamson as forming part of the evidence for the making of the assessment was the actual turnover of the business for the relevant year which, he says, was taken from Studio's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2020 which were filed with Companies House in January 2021.
Mr Williamson accepted that these figures were not needed before HMRC could make an assessment as the assessment could have been made on the basis of provisional figures (ie the turnover figures shown in the 19 December 2021 calculations).
However, as we have seen, that is not the test. The question is what facts were relied on by the relevant HMRC officer in making the assessment which was actually made and not a different assessment which could have been made but which was not.
It is clear that HMRC needed to have evidence of the actual turnover of the business in order to make the assessment which was in fact made on 1 October 2021 as it was based on those figures. The fact that HMRC could have made best judgment assessments based on the turnover figures used in the 19 December 2021 calculations is irrelevant.
We should mention that when HMRC's assessment decision was reviewed, the review officer mentioned in their conclusions that HMRC had relied on turnover figures purportedly appended to PwC’s letter of 30 April 2021 when making the original assessment. Mr Williamson’s evidence is that this is wrong and that the figures in fact came from the statutory accounts as mentioned above.
It is clear that Mr Williamson is correct that no reliance was placed on any turnover figures attached to the letter from PwC dated 30 April 2021 as there were no such figures contained in the appendix to that letter which, instead, simply set out the input tax incurred on the photography and modelling costs (and not the turnover of the business).
Whilst Ms Sloane is critical of HMRC for making this mistake in the review letter, in our view it has no bearing on the question we have to decide which is identifying the evidence which, in the opinion of the assessing officer, justified the assessment.
Based on what we have said above, we find that the final piece of the jigsaw was received by HMRC on 30 April 2021. At that point, Mr Williamson (and therefore Mr Hughes as the assessing officer) had all of the information which, in his opinion, justified the making of the assessment which was issued on 1 October 2021. This assessment was not therefore made out of time.
Turning to the assessment made on 30 March 2022 relating to the 03/20 VAT period Studio's position is that HMRC had enough information to make the assessment as soon as it had submitted its VAT return on 24 April 2020 given that by that time HMRC already knew from the information that had been provided in December 2019 that not all of the exempt interest had been included in the apportionment calculations.
For the reasons set out above, we do not accept this. One piece of information received by HMRC which justified the making of the assessment, being the reason for the 12 month restriction on interest, was only received on 30 April 2021. The assessment on 30 March 2022 was made less than a year after that information was received and was not therefore made out of time.
In any event, Mr Williamson’s evidence is that HMRC needed to see the calculations that lay behind the figures in the VAT return for the 03/20 VAT period before making any decision in relation to an assessment. That information was provided on 29 November 2021.
The need for this information was not challenged by Ms Sloane in cross-examination. Although Mr Williamson confirmed that he could not speak to the assessing officer’s own opinion in respect of this information, for the reasons we have already explained, we infer that the assessing officer shared Mr Williamson's views.
The result of that is that as far as the assessment dated 30 March 2022 in respect of the 03/20 VAT period is concerned, the last piece of evidence was in fact only obtained on 29 November 2021. As this was only four months before the assessment was made, it was within the time limit in s 73(6)(b) VATA.
Summary of conclusions
The photography and modelling costs have a direct and immediate link not only with the taxable supply of goods but also the exempt supply of credit. They are therefore residual costs which fall to be apportioned along with the other residual marketing costs.
Whilst not perfect, the standard turnover method is fair and reasonable and does not give rise to significant distortions. The alternatives put forward by Studio do not guarantee a more precise result.
The assessments for the VAT periods 09/19 and 03/20 were made within the relevant time limit.
Studio's appeals against the various assessments and against HMRC’s decisions are therefore dismissed in their entirety.
Right to apply for permission to appeal
This document contains full findings of fact and reasons for the decision. Any party dissatisfied with this decision has a right to apply for permission to appeal against it pursuant to Rule 39 of the Tribunal Procedure (First-tier Tribunal) (Tax Chamber) Rules 2009. The application must be received by this Tribunal not later than 56 days after this decision is sent to that party. The parties are referred to “Guidance to accompany a Decision from the First-tier Tribunal (Tax Chamber)” which accompanies and forms part of this decision notice.

items.title: Company fined for providing false electrical safety certificates for car washes
items.summary: Two car wash companies in Runcorn found to be unsafe and ordered to stop work Company hired to carry out repairs issued false certificates declaring they were safe Sites continuing operating despite electrocution risks to workers and members of the public A company has been fined after it falsely supplied electrical safety certificates to two […]
items.body:
- Two car wash companies in Runcorn found to be unsafe and ordered to stop work
- Company hired to carry out repairs issued false certificates declaring they were safe
- Sites continuing operating despite electrocution risks to workers and members of the public
A company has been fined after it falsely supplied electrical safety certificates to two car wash businesses in Runcorn, despite them both being declared unsafe.
Inspectors from Britain’s workplace regulator – alongside colleagues from Cheshire Police, Trading Standards and the immigration authorities – carried out an investigation into the activities of Super Hand Car Wash on Halton Road and Top Star Hand Car Wash on Bridge Street.
Both premises were found to have electrical systems that were dangerous. This resulted in Health and Safety Executive (HSE) inspectors taking enforcement action against both businesses – forcing them to immediately stop work. The car wash owners were advised to use a National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting (NICEIC) registered electrical contractor or similar, to ensure that electrics were made safe to ensure the safety of the public and the people working on site.
Epco Energy Solutions Limited, who were at the time, members of the NICEIC were engaged to carry out the work and certified the installations as being safe to use.
However, an examination of the certificates by one of HSE’s specialist electrical inspectors found that details in them did not match the installations he found on site. A subsequent visit to both car washes found that the installations were still dangerous and presented a risk of serious injury or electrocution to those on site, including members of the public.
The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require all electrical installations to be maintained in a safe condition. This means that systems should only be worked on by someone who is a competent electrical contractor. The NICEIC is one of the certification bodies for electrical contractors in the UK. Membership of such a body indicates that the member has received appropriate training, and has been assessed to ensure that they are competent to carry out work on electrical systems. HSE guidance on electrical safety is available. Electrical safety – HSE
Epco Energy Solutions Limited had visited and provided electronically generated certificates using the NICEIC secure members only systems. Certificates provided to the car washes indicated that the electrical systems on site were safe to use when they were not. With support from the NICEIC it was found that the certificates had been generated using password protected software and electronically signed with sole Epco Director Mohammed Naeem’s signature.
Epco Energy Solutions Limited, of Unit B, 37 Worlsey Road, Eccles, Manchester, were found guilty after a trial at Warrington Magistrates Court on 2 September 2026, of breaching section 3(1) of the Health and Safety At Work Act 1974 etc, 1974. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £15,239 at the same court on 22 October 2026.
HSE inspector Rose Leese-Weller said:
“Due to having such a close relationship with water, car wash owners must ensure that their electrical installations are maintained in a safe condition.
“As well as being safe to use they must also be fit for purpose so as to prevent serious personal injury or electrocution to anyone in the vicinity.
“These car washes where dangerous and unsafe – to both those working there and to members of the public visiting the sites.
“Electrical installations at all workplaces must be maintained in a safe condition and are safe to use.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by enforcement lawyer Sam Crockett and paralegal officer Hettie Burrows.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- Relevant guidance can be found here – Electrical safety – HSE.

items.title: Fine for manufacturing company after man left as ‘a shadow of his former self’
items.summary: Gary Taylor, suffered multiple injuries when he was hit on the head by a one- tonne metal hopper He spent three weeks in hospital and had to take seven months off work E H Hassell & Sons Limited fined £300,000 for failing to properly plan for work A Staffordshire-based manufacturing company has been fined £300,000 […]
items.body:
- Gary Taylor, suffered multiple injuries when he was hit on the head by a one- tonne metal hopper
- He spent three weeks in hospital and had to take seven months off work
- E H Hassell & Sons Limited fined £300,000 for failing to properly plan for work
A Staffordshire-based manufacturing company has been fined £300,000 after a family man was left with injuries so serious he became ‘a shadow of his former self’.
Gary Taylor, who was 63 at the time, spent three weeks in hospital and needed seven months off work, following the incident on 24 March 2025.
The grandfather had been working for E H Hassell & Sons Limited at its site on Newstead Ind Estate in Trentham. He was one of several workers involved in the unloading of a lorry trailer containing various steel components for a large filtration system.
The workers had improvised a system to unload the metal hopper with a forklift truck, placing the forks underneath the unsecured load to lift it from the trailer bed. However, as it slid from the forks, it struck Mr Taylor in the head as he was stood alongside it. His injuries included fractures to his skull, neck and spine, two broken ribs and a severe laceration to his forehead which required 17 staples and 14 stitches.
Mr Taylor described how the incident has had a lasting impact on his life.
“During my time off recuperating from my injuries, the seven months I was off work, I had no interest in anything,” he said.
“I know my wife thinks that I won’t be around with her in my eighties, she has constant worry that something is going to happen to me.
“She never thought like that before my accident.
“For me, I have no idea what the future holds.
“I can only hope that I will get better as time goes on and I become more like the old man I used to be – a supportive husband, father and grandfather to my grandchildren.
“I want to be a person that hopefully will become more of a person than a shadow of my former self.”
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the lifting operation had not been properly planned by a competent person. The characteristics of the load, including its weight, size, centre of gravity and lifting points, had not been adequately assessed, and no safe system of work had been put in place.
Moving an object of this size and weight was not a regular task at the site and there was no established system of work for it.
HSE guidance on Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE states that it is important to properly resource, plan and organise lifting operations so they are carried out in a safe manner.
E H Hassell & Sons Limited of Alderflat Drive, Trentham, Staffordshire pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 8(1) of the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 and were fined £300,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,690 at a hearing at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.
HSE inspector Claire Whitehurst said:
“The failures here resulted in an experienced worker suffering life-changing injuries.
“The company failed to properly plan the lifting operation or implement a safe system of work.
“Mr Taylor suffered serious injuries which could easily have resulted in his death. He has been left with facial scarring, and both he and his family have been deeply affected by this traumatic experience.
“Employers must ensure that lifting operations are properly planned by a competent person and carried out safely. This is especially important for non-routine tasks involving heavy or awkward loads.”
The HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer, Julian White and supported by HSE paralegal officer, Stephen Grabe. The investigation was supported by visiting officer, Natalka Heath.

- Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited had failed to consider impact of changes it had made to workplace transport routes
CCTV has captured the moment a young worker was injured when the ride-on pallet truck he was using collided with a fork lift truck in a warehouse in Yorkshire.
Bed spring manufacturer Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited has been fined after Charlie O’Dowd was injured in the incident at its Long Royd warehouse in Barnsley on 14 November 2024.
The then 20-year-old had been using a ride-on pallet truck during the installation of new automated machinery within the warehouse. However, his truck, which was unguarded, collided with a fork lift truck being driven by another employee, resulting in multiple fractures to his foot, as well as longer term nerve damage.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had made changes to its workplace transport routes to accommodate the installation works taking place. However, these changes meant that both ride-on pallet trucks and fork lift trucks were required to use the same routes, within what was a busy stock loading area. Visibility was limited and vehicle movements had increased.
The HSE investigation concluded that the company had focused on the installation of the new machinery but had failed to adequately consider the impact that significant changes to workplace transport arrangements would have on worker safety. The changes to vehicle routes had not been properly risk assessed before being implemented.
Every year, there are accidents involving transport in the workplace, some of which result in people being killed. HSE guidance explains what should be done to keep workers safe – Introduction to workplace transport safety – HSE.
Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited, pleaded guilty to a breach of Section 2(1) of the Health & Safey at Work etc. Act 1974 in relation to the safe use of workplace transport within the warehouse. The company was fined £80,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £3,374 at Leeds Magistrates Court on 20 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Chris Parker said:
“This case highlights the importance of carefully assessing the wider safety implications of any changes made within a workplace, even where those changes may be temporary.
“When workplace transport routes are altered, employers must ensure that the risks created by those changes are properly assessed and controlled before they are introduced.
“Had suitable planning and risk assessment been carried out, this incident could have been prevented.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Zara Salman and advocacy undertaken by enforcement lawyer Arfaq Nabi.

items.title: Half-a-million pound fine for company after worker suffers 40 per cent burns
items.summary: Three-tonne steel beam fell into bath of molten zinc that created wave that covered worker 33-year-old man spent 11 days in intensive care requiring 13 operations Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited fined more than £500k after HSE investigation finds chains used to lift beam were damaged and deteriorated One of Britain’s leading steel galvanizers has been […]
items.body:
- Three-tonne steel beam fell into bath of molten zinc that created wave that covered worker
- 33-year-old man spent 11 days in intensive care requiring 13 operations
- Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited fined more than £500k after HSE investigation finds chains used to lift beam were damaged and deteriorated
One of Britain’s leading steel galvanizers has been fined more than £500,000 after one of its workers suffered 40 per cent burns to his body when hit by a wave of molten zinc at its site in Devon.
The employee was working for Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited at its site in Marsh End, Lords Meadow Industrial Estate in Crediton, Mid Devon, when the incident happened on 12 October 2021.
Hot dip galvanizing is a process that provides long-term protection against rust and corrosion of steel products. On the day in question, a lifting chain, carrying a roller steel joist weighing nearly three tonnes, failed. The beam fell into a galvanizing bath and the resulting wave of molten zinc covered the 33-year-old, before hitting a wall and surging back along the floor towards him.
CCTV footage from the scene shows the worker alight and running towards the emergency shower where his clothes were removed and he was doused in water. He was initially treated at the scene by paramedics, before being taken by air ambulance to Southmead hospital in Bristol. He had suffered 40 per cent burns and remained in intensive care for 11 days undergoing 13 separate operations. Any remaining healthy skin was grafted to repair his burnt body.
During his lengthy treatment the man suffered infection and sepsis leaving him with multiple long-term health conditions.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the set of chains used to lift the heavy steel beam had signs of damage and deterioration and there was a failure to withdraw them. Crucially, the chains had not undergone their mandatory regular inspection.
The investigation also revealed that the load slinging arrangement used at the time of the incident was incorrect, which meant that the load being lifted was greater than the safe limit for the chains. The risk assessment in place at the time of the incident for “immersion & swilling” had no reference to checks on chains, or what type of sling configuration to use.
Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited failed to meet several regulations and standards. Under the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations (LOLER) 1998, lifting accessories must be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least every six months. Both the Lifting Equipment Engineers Association (LEEA) code of practice and the user manual for the chain manufacturer state that chain slings used in acidic environments, such as zinc galvanising, should be inspected before each day’s use.
The Health and Safety Executive publishes freely available guidance which underlines the importance of thorough inspection of lifting equipment, including the benefits of an ‘examination scheme’.
Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited of Stafford Street, Willenhall, West Midlands, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £566,666 and ordered to pay £15,521 in costs at Bristol Magistrates Court on Wednesday 14 October 2026.
HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said:
“This wholly-avoidable incident led to a young man having to endure truly terrible injuries – and the disturbing truth is that the consequences could have been even worse.
“It is shocking that an industry-leading firm,, with considerable resources at its disposal, should risk the lives of its workers with substandard inspection protocols.
“Our thoughts are with the victim at the heart of this incident, his friends and family, and all those at the site who have been affected by what happened that day.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Gemma Zakrzewski, Paralegal Officer, Farhat Basir and Rowena Goodwin, Enforcement Advocate.
